1	<!-- What Pavol, the curator, knows, graded by topic, for pitching an explanation or an ask at him, with each line's evidence in PROFILE-sources.md beside it. -->
2	
3	# What Pavol knows
4	
5	A topic reads `topic — level — how to pitch it`. `1 → 3` is a level that rose: pitch at the later one.
6	
7	- 4, expert: hands-on depth; talk as to a peer.
8	- 3, working: uses it correctly; no explanation, define only the project's own terms.
9	- 2, familiar: knows the idea, not the details; a one-line reminder before it is used.
10	- 1, heard of: knows the name; explain it with one concrete case before using it.
11	- 0, new: explain from the ground up, concrete cases first, with the shortest grounding that worked where there is one.
12	
13	## Topics
14	
15	### Languages and tools
16	
17	- Benchmarking and measurement statistics — 4 — talk as to a peer; frame speed results this way.
18	- Swift as a library and benchmark writer — 3 — his first frame; its compiler's insides, and its names for unique references and copy-on-write, are 1.
19	- Scala (2.8 era), Java and the JVM, Python, iOS, as a user — 3 — take as known; their compilers' insides are new.
20	- Rust, Julia, Kotlin, Clojure, C++ templates — 2 — one line on the peer's idea; Clojure's multimethods are 1.
21	- What generators cost against a loop — 3 — he measured it himself; use it for big operators.
22	- APL — 0 — the side quest is closed.
23	
24	### Types and language design
25	
26	- Type theory, formally — 0 — a concrete Fortress program and several cases before any rule.
27	- Dispatch on all arguments; exclusions; coercion against subtyping; `Any` against `Object` — 1 → 3 — take as known.
28	- The checker's overload rules — 1 — the idea stuck, the rules didn't; show concrete pairs of declarations.
29	- Erased against kept generics; traits that give behavior; a subtype with its own operation — 3 — he judges by ergonomics and reuse, not purity.
30	- `where` clauses; soundness — 0 → 2 — remind him that `where` narrows where a declaration applies.
31	- `nat` size parameters — 0 → 2 — remind him that a `nat` is a size the type carries; arithmetic on sizes is 0.
32	- An interface against a trait — 1 — he is unsure of the words; say "extends".
33	
34	### Mathematics
35	
36	- Matrix and vector products, the dot product — 1 — he knows only that inner dimensions match; start from a 2×2 matrix times a vector, show that order matters, then C4's shapes: 16×16 (attention), 27×16 (token table), 64×16 (feed-forward).
37	- Rings, fields, additive groups — 0 — no grounding has worked yet.
38	- Identity elements on each type's algebra — 3 — take as known.
39	- Q, Z and N; `ZZ` signed, `NN` not — 0 → 3 — take as known.
40	- The library's number types — 2 — bottom up, `ZZ32` first; top down failed.
41	- Floating point — 2 — he knows IEEE rounding against Java's; infinities among the rationals were new.
42	- Reshape, ravel, outer product, tensor — 0 — define each on a small array.
43	- Mathematical notation — 1 — set it beside the Fortress code that computes it.
44	
45	### Machine learning
46	
47	- micrograd, microGPT, nanoGPT; FP32; integer tokens — 3 — take as known; microGPT's baseline is CPython or NumPy.
48	- KV cache, loss curves, early stopping, Chinchilla — 2 — a one-line reminder.
49	- Backpropagation, functional or tape-style, and its cost — 1 — his views are guesses.
50	- Big operators as ML papers write them — 1 — "hardly a yardstick", he says.
51	- Attention and softmax — 0 — learning them was microGPT's point for him; teach from C4's code.
52	
53	### Fortress, its sources and the record
54	
55	- Steele's talks: juxtaposition, undefined precedence, parallel loops, inference, units, `Σ` over new types — 3 — take as known.
56	- Where intent lives: the papers, the TeX not the PDF, the team's later word, the library among the sources — 3 — his rules.
57	- Who did what: Ryu's front end, Park's POPL 2019 paper — 3 — take as known.
58	- The library's shape: `Vector` and `Matrix` for numbers only — 2 — a one-line reminder.
59	- The specification, the papers, the library's text — 1 — unread; quote the line that decides.
60	- Reading Fortress code — 1 → 2 — he reads a declaration line by line; gloss each new construct.
61	- `label` and `exit`, `comprises`, `atomic`, `thrower`, `reflect`, DSL blocks, where whitespace counts — 0 — one concrete case each.
62	- FACTS, POSITIONS, the original protocol — 0 — never read; say what an entry says.
63	- Walk against the compiled path; the compiler's prelude — 0 → 3 — take as known.
64	
65	### Compilers and run times
66	
67	- JVM performance: boxing, the JIT, specialization, unboxed doubles — 1 → 3 — where he grew most.
68	- The pipeline, the caches, JVM array limits, warm-up, races hidden by one thread — 3 — take as known.
69	- Loom, the Vector API, Truffle, GraalVM — 0 → 2 — a one-line reminder.
70	- The class loader and its descriptors — 0 → 2 — from his own picture: sizes stamped into a class, as Swift mangles names, so the JIT drops bounds checks.
71	- One-time facts: which phases run the checker, the earlier compiler, a coercion's cost at run time, a load of 30 — 1 — one line when it comes up.
72	- The checker count and the distance to the switch-over — 1 — each time: what each counts, and why one can jump.
73	
74	### The repository and the process
75	
76	- Git; Claude Code's client; test-first, with `XXX` tests until a fix flips them — 3 — take as known.
77	- The platform: remote sessions, secrets in a container, the weekly reset — 1 — one line when it matters.
78	- The project's own terms; his past rulings — 2 — he forgets them after a gap; restate them by content.
79	- POSITIONS, "History he knows", and his decisions — 3 — take as known; cite a decision by what it says, never by its number.
80	- The coordinator's three principles — 1 — he knows the nine-step form, not these.
81	
82	## How to explain to him
83	
84	- Pitch at a software engineer who directs the work, not a researcher. Say what a feature costs.
85	- Concrete cases before the rule: several, on C4 or a Fortress program. He checks them for a contradiction, then takes the rule.
86	- Frame in what he knows, his own analogies first: the complex-number Mandelbrot, the diagonal matrix, Swift's debug builds, LLVM's lit.
87	- Define each term where it is used.
88	- Show Fortress code as Fortress, infix, not calls. Set notation beside the code. Draw a picture where structure matters.
89	- An ask: the question, context with a primer, numbered options with trade-offs and none that does nothing, the ask, the recommendation last. On types: the specification and the team's later word first, then the library, then the peers as context only. Say what each option does for a fast microGPT.
90	- One ask at a time, answerable as "3b". Show the wording before a yes. Mark a decision surfaced for his learning as one.
91	- Length by mode: three lines and "holding" while he reads turn by turn; an ask 1.5K to 3.3K, 5K with a refresher; long only to establish facts, never unasked.
92	- If he answers a long turn piece by piece: hold, list his points, and wait.
93	- When he's tired: one item, a default he can take, an offer to come back to it.
94	- When he ends "how wrong am I?": answer it, and reflect his idea back refined.
95	- He reads fast and forgets: restate, don't refer back.
96	- Plain words, halfway to ASD-STE100, positive phrasing.
97	- The phone, with Speak: a Select button per section, links not paths, no tables, numbers as K and M. A stop can be an accidental tap.
98	- Dictation: repair a term silently unless two readings differ. Seen, as heard → meant: forty five → Fortify, contact → compact, WordPress → Fortress, Table → Fable, scalar → Scala, Perl → parallel, Docker → checker, time system → type system, rank → rung, net → nat, Sue → Hsu, Popple → POPL, 16 → 64.
99	
100	## Words to avoid
101	
102	- A bare label: "P1", "row 40", "answer 9", "the judge", "the line". Name the thing.
103	- "Closure" for the integer tower; "sealed" for `Σ`; "revising the specification" for reconciling its contradictions.
104	- "Tensor", "reshape", "ravel", "outer product", "ring", "field", undefined; "coercion" for "conversion".
105	- "Yesterday"; "we" for him and Claude; a coda, a slogan, a clever turn.
106	
107	## Open contradictions
108	
109	- Length: he demands short replies, yet praised a long one while facts were being established.
110	- Reading: he says he hasn't read the specification or the library, yet spot-checks them and recalls Steele's talks exactly.
111	- Type theory: he says he knows none, yet reasons soundly about coercion, bounds and erasure.
112	- Scala: he says it earned his Stack Overflow points; most of the account is iOS.
113	- Peers: he asks what they do, yet rules that they only decide between the designers' choices; "context only" is the record's reading.
114	- Ownership: he wants every choice, yet at times takes a default unread.
115	- History: he recalls `main` as free of the third-party port; the record says otherwise.
116	- Other languages: his claims about them are unchecked; check one before building on it.
117

1	<!-- The text of the teaching page "Arrays in Fortress", written on 2026-11-17 by a delegated Opus worker of the coordinating session for Pavol, the curator, at his questions on arrays after climb batch 33 was planned: how an array is written and typed, which part is syntax and which library, how the nat sizes ride in the type on each path, where the elements live, what boxing costs, what the switch-over rehearsal ran and why its loop was slow, the work before the first array program runs on the one library, his array decisions decided and open, and the older array reports marked current or out of date; every program ran under walk in a scratch worktree seeded from the base build at c3b16ef2d1 and removed after, and no timing was taken. -->
2	
3	*Fortress revival · a teaching page · 17 November 2026*
4	
5	# Arrays in Fortress
6	
7	You asked how arrays work, how the rehearsal ran them with no array decision taken, and what stands before an array program runs. This page goes from small programs up to the design. Each program on it ran today under walk, the interpreter, and its output is shown as it printed.
8	
9	## 1. The short answers
10	
11	- **The first array program to run** is the smallest of the switch-over rehearsal, a trial in a throwaway tree. The switch-over moves the compiled path, the compile to JVM bytecode, onto the one library, the interpreter’s library. The program makes an array of 8 `ZZ32` with the library’s factory, writes `i i` into each element, and prints `a[5] = 25`. After the second run, the second launch, of the batch now landing, it compiles against the one library. It runs in the batch after, once that library compiles whole to bytecode.
12	- **You need to do nothing now.** An array is library code: Fortress traits and objects over a store, the object that holds the elements. The compiler compiles it as it compiles any library code. The open array decisions are about speed and the model’s own types, not about running.
13	- **Half language, half library.** The literal `[1 2 3]` and the shorthand `ZZ32[3]` are the language’s. The types behind them, `Array1`, `Vector` and `Matrix`, are the library’s.
14	- **The sizes ride in the type on both paths.** Walk checks them as a line runs. The compiled checker checks them before the compile.
15	- **Every element today is boxed**, a number wrapped in a heap object. The bare-double store that “nothing chooses” is the team’s immutable `RR64` array: no factory returns it.
16	- **The rehearsal’s loop was about 100 times slower than Java.** Boxing explains 6 to 7 of that. The rest has no measured share.
17	- **Boxed numbers now change no array decision.** A bare-double store alone buys nothing while each read still makes a box.
18	
19	**References**
20	
21	1. The program, its compile and its run: [CLIMB-BATCH-33.md](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-33.md), section 2, “R. A method found by its interface”, “The measures” and “For the batch after, in this order”, item 4. The rest: the sections below.
22	
23	## 2. An array, written and typed
24	
25	Start from the specification’s example, with a few lines added. `typecase` takes the first arm whose type matches the value as it runs, like Swift’s `switch` with `case is T`.
26	
27	```
28	A: ZZ32[3,3] = [1 2 3; 4 5 6; 7 8 9]
29	println("A[1,0] = " A[1,0])
30	println("|A| = " |A|)
31	v: RR64[3] = [1.0 2.0 3.0]
32	println("v DOT v = " (v DOT v))
33	typecase v of
34	  Vector[\RR64,3\] => println("v is a Vector[\\RR64,3\\]")
35	  else => println("v is no vector")
36	end
37	s: String[2] = ["ab" "cd"]
38	typecase s of
39	  AnyVector => println("s is a vector")
40	  Array1[\String,0,2\] => println("s is an Array1[\\String,0,2\\], no vector")
41	  else => println("s is something else")
42	end
43	```
44	
45	*Under walk, it printed:*
46	
47	```
48	A[1,0] = 4
49	|A| = 9
50	v DOT v = 14.0
51	v is a Vector[\RR64,3\]
52	s is an Array1[\String,0,2\], no vector
53	```
54	
55	- Spaces separate the elements of a row. A semicolon or a new line separates rows, and two semicolons separate the planes of a 3-dimensional array.
56	- `ZZ32[3,3]` is the specification’s shorthand for `Array2[\ZZ32, 0, 3, 0, 3\]`: for each dimension, a lowest index, 0, and a size, 3. That’s the notation on the number type that you saw.
57	- `A[1,0]` is row 1, column 0, counted from 0.
58	- One literal syntax gave a matrix, a `Vector` and a plain `Array1`. The specification lets the context decide. The library’s factory decides, by testing the element type against the eight number types.
59	- The overview’s `RR^3`, a vector of 3, isn’t built. Walk reads it as a type of its own. Today `v: RR64^3 = [1.0 2.0 3.0]` bound, and the `println(v)` after it stopped: “Couldn’t figure out Matrix [\RR64\]^(3) <: Object”.
60	
61	**References**
62	
63	1. The literal, its type and the shorthand: [aggregate.tex](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex#L117-L137), lines 117 to 137; the example, [Expr.Array.a.fss](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/SpecData/examples/basic/Expr.Array.a.fss).
64	2. The context decides, and `T^n`: [overview.tex](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/Specification/preliminaries/overview.tex#L735-L773), lines 735 to 773 and 934 to 938; [Overview.Expression.aggregate.a.fss](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/SpecData/examples/preliminaries/Overview.Expression.aggregate.a.fss), [Overview.Moving.fss](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/SpecData/examples/preliminaries/Overview.Moving.fss).
65	3. The factory’s test: [FortressLibrary.fss](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/Library/FortressLibrary.fss#L2842-L2856), lines 2842 to 2856; FACTS F-229.
66	4. `T^n` under walk: gap ledger row 24. The stopped `println` is today’s run, a shape that the row doesn’t name.
67	5. The run: `Literal.fss`, by `bin/fortress` in a worktree seeded from the base build at `c3b16ef2d1`, whose library equals `main`’s at `9f2ff9b04e`.
68	
69	## 3. The syntax is the language’s, the types are the library’s
70	
71	You took the array types for library types, and the literals for built-in syntax. Both are right. The language, its parser and walk, give:
72	
73	- the literal, `[1 2 3; 4 5 6]`, and the shorthand `T[n, m]`;
74	- the subscript forms `a[i]`, `a[i, j]` and `a[i] := v`;
75	- static parameters, `[\T, nat n\]`, where `nat` marks a size that the type carries.
76	
77	The library gives:
78	
79	- `Array[\E, I\]`, with no size in its type. `I` is the index type: `ZZ32`, or a pair for rank 2.
80	- `Array1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]`, `Array2` and `Array3`, with a lowest index and a size for each dimension.
81	- `Vector` and `Matrix`, for numbers only, with their arithmetic.
82	- the factories `array1[\T, n\]()`, `vector`, `matrix`, and `array[\T\](n)` for a size known only when the program runs.
83	- the subscript itself: `a[i]` calls the operator `opr[i:I]:E = get(offset(i))`, as Swift’s `a[i]` calls the type’s `subscript`.
84	
85	They meet at two names that walk knows: `Array` plus the rank, and `__builtinFactory` plus the rank. For `[1 2 3]` at a declared type, walk calls `__builtinFactory1[\ZZ32, 0, 3\]()` and copies the elements in. A literal with no declared type isn’t built today.
86	
87	`Array1` isn’t in a component that you import, as `List` is. It’s in `FortressLibrary`, which every program sees.
88	
89	In your frames: Swift’s `[Double]` is shorthand for the standard library’s `Array<Double>`. `RR64[3]` is shorthand for the library’s `Array1[\RR64,0,3\]`, with the size in the type. Scala’s compiler makes `Array[Double]` a JVM `double[]`. Fortress has no such special case yet.
90	
91	**References**
92	
93	1. 98	
99	The library’s rank-1 array keeps no length field. It reads the size from its type:

102	trait ReadableArray1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\] ...
103	    opr |self| : ZZ32 = s0
104	    offset(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = do
105	        r = i - b0
106	        if NOT (0 <= r < s0) then oops(1, b0, s0, i) end
107	        r
108	    end
109	```

223	## 6. Boxing, and what it costs
224	
225	A boxed number is held in a heap object. On the compiled path an `RR64` is an object of the Java class `FRR64`, with one `double` field: Java’s `Double` against `double`. Today the code generator boxes every number, so a compiled `RR64` loop holds no `dadd` or `dmul`.
226	
227	Java models of the compiled boxes, against `double[]`:
228	
229	- a dot product over 4K elements: 6.3 times;
230	- a 16-by-16 matrix product: 6.5 times;
231	- the row lift, a function applied to each row: 2.6 times.
232	
233	An `Object[]` behind an interface, with a cast on each read, added only 1.6 to 9 %. The boxes cost, the generic container doesn’t. In a hot loop the JIT removes a temporary box that doesn’t escape. An array element escapes, since it’s stored, so its box stays.
234	
235	A `double[]` store alone buys nothing while each read still makes a box. In the Java model, a dot product over a `double[]` read through a boxing accessor ran at 8.9 times the bare loop, against 6.4 for boxed storage. So where the elements live and where the reads and arithmetic run unboxed are two decisions.
236	
237	“Boxed numbers now” means this. Your decision makes each built-in number type one value object, an object without identity that no type can extend, so that compiled code can later hold a `ZZ32` as a bare `int`. In the batch’s second run, one change writes each prelude number type’s class over a small hand-written class that holds the bare value. Code still passes boxes until the unboxing work, in the phase in which microGPT runs fast.
238	
239	For arrays that changes no decision. Your decision fixes the goal: each number type’s array stored unboxed, in a Java array of its primitive type, with the sizes in the types now. In your words: “All arrays must have the most efficient and performant implementation possible. Otherwise it will remain a research toy, not an HPC language.”

3The syntax is the language’s, the types are the library’s

148

You took the array types for library types, and the literals for built-in syntax. Both are right. The language, its parser and walk, give:

149
    150
  • the literal, [1 2 3; 4 5 6], and the shorthand T[n, m];
    • 151
  • the subscript forms a[i], a[i, j] and a[i] := v;
    • 152
  • static parameters, [\T, nat n\], where nat marks a size that the type carries.
    • 153
154

The library gives:

155
    156
  • Array[\E, I\], with no size in its type. I is the index type: ZZ32, or a pair for rank 2.
    • 157
  • Array1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\], Array2 and Array3, with a lowest index and a size for each dimension.
    • 158
  • Vector and Matrix, for numbers only, with their arithmetic.
    • 159
  • the factories array1[\T, n\](), vector, matrix, and array[\T\](n) for a size known only when the program runs.
    • 160
  • the subscript itself: a[i] calls the operator opr[i:I]:E = get(offset(i)), as Swift’s a[i] calls the type’s subscript.
    • 161
162

They meet at two names that walk knows: Array plus the rank, and __builtinFactory plus the rank. For [1 2 3] at a declared type, walk calls __builtinFactory1[\ZZ32, 0, 3\]() and copies the elements in. A literal with no declared type isn’t built today.

163

Array1 isn’t in a component that you import, as List is. It’s in FortressLibrary, which every program sees.

164

In your frames: Swift’s [Double] is shorthand for the standard library’s Array<Double>. RR64[3] is shorthand for the library’s Array1[\RR64,0,3\], with the size in the type. Scala’s compiler makes Array[Double] a JVM double[]. Fortress has no such special case yet.

4How the sizes ride in the type

176

The library’s rank-1 array keeps no length field. It reads the size from its type:

177 
trait ReadableArray1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\] ...
178	    opr |self| : ZZ32 = s0
179	    offset(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = do
180	        r = i - b0
181	        if NOT (0 <= r < s0) then oops(1, b0, s0, i) end
182	        r
183	    end
184

A product names a shared size once, so the shapes must match. An n-by-m matrix times a vector of m gives a vector of n:

185 
opr juxtaposition[\T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat n, nat m\]
186	    (me: Matrix[\T,n,m\], v: Vector[\T,m\]): Vector[\T,n\]

  • Walk keeps the sizes in each object’s type: __DefaultVector[\RR64,3\] is the library’s vector object at size 3. As it makes the object, walk binds each nat parameter to its number, so a body reads s0 as a value. It finds a mismatch only when the line runs.

  • The compiled checker refuses a mismatch before the compile. Two sizes are equal when written alike once numerals are computed: 2 3 equals 6, but m n doesn’t equal n m.

The class loader makes each instance’s class at first use, with the sizes in its name: the rehearsal’s trace names __DefaultMatrix⟦FRR64,3,4⟧. Each size has one descriptor object, for type tests. Where a body reads s0, the loader writes in the constant, FZZ32.make(3). That’s your picture: sizes stamped into a class, as Swift mangles names. No optimization reads a size yet.

5Where the elements live today

241

A Vector[\RR64,3\] from array1 is three objects deep. The vector, __DefaultVector, holds a PrimitiveArray. That holds a store, a JavaArrayStore. The store holds the elements in Java. A 2-by-3 matrix holds one store of s0 s1 cells, 6, row by row: a size can be a product.

242
    243
  • Under walk, the store is walk’s own AtomicArray of walk’s boxed values.
    • 244
  • Compiled against the one library, as in the rehearsal, it’s the Java class FortressArrayStore, an Object[] of boxes such as FRR64. Inside atomic, each read and write of an element goes through the transaction.
    • 245
  • Compiled against the prelude, the compiler’s own small library, which main still uses by default, there’s no array type at all: “Array1 is undefined”.
    • 246

The store over a bare double array is in PrimImmutableRR64Array, the team’s immutable RR64 array in the one library’s NativeArray. Walk holds its elements in a double[], and so does its compiled class, FortressRR64ArrayStore. It has get and init, no put. “Nothing chooses it” means this:

The store works, and the factory doesn’t pick it. How a factory picks each element type’s store is your first open question.

The prelude’s native arrays are something else. The prelude has ZZ32Vector, over a Java int[], and StringVector, over a String[]. The team wrote both by hand in August 2011. 6Boxing, and what it costs

275

A boxed number is held in a heap object. On the compiled path an RR64 is an object of the Java class FRR64, with one double field: Java’s Double against double. Today the code generator boxes every number, so a compiled RR64 loop holds no dadd or dmul.

276

Java models of the compiled boxes, against double[]:

277
    278
  • a dot product over 4K elements: 6.3 times;
    • 279
  • a 16-by-16 matrix product: 6.5 times;
    • 280
  • the row lift, a function applied to each row: 2.6 times.
    • 281
282

An Object[] behind an interface, with a cast on each read, added only 1.6 to 9 %. The boxes cost, the generic container doesn’t. In a hot loop the JIT removes a temporary box that doesn’t escape. An array element escapes, since it’s stored, so its box stays.

283

A double[] store alone buys nothing while each read still makes a box. In the Java model, a dot product over a double[] read through a boxing accessor ran at 8.9 times the bare loop, against 6.4 for boxed storage. So where the elements live and where the reads and arithmetic run unboxed are two decisions.

284

“Boxed numbers now” means this. Your decision makes each built-in number type one value object, an object without identity that no type can extend, so that compiled code can later hold a ZZ32 as a bare int. In the batch’s second run, one change writes each prelude number type’s class over a small hand-written class that holds the bare value. Code still passes boxes until the unboxing work, in the phase in which microGPT runs fast.

285

For arrays that changes no decision. Your decision fixes the goal: each number type’s array stored unboxed, in a Java array of its primitive type, with the sizes in the types now. In your words: “All arrays must have the most efficient and performant implementation possible. Otherwise it will remain a research toy, not an HPC language.”

298

The switch-over rehearsal of 10 November worked in a scratch tree, a throwaway copy where nothing lands. Two lines pointed its compiled path at the one library, and twelve marked hacks passed the walls that a hack could pass. The library’s 14 components compiled to bytecode in about 200 s. Then the array program printed a[5] = 25, and a dot product in the program’s own loop printed dot = 499500.0. The library’s DOT and a matrix died at two walls, fixed since. microGPT’s flat program stopped at the checker, mostly on its arrays without sizes. Probe Y, a second trial on 13 November, ran the same programs in one build that serves either library by one setting. The batch now landing puts that setting on main: FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one.

So about 160 ns an iteration against about 1 ns. It’s one run each, in different sessions at different loads, with the JIT’s warm-up inside and the verifier off: an order of magnitude, no more.

8From here to an array program that runs

333

18

30	## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over
31	
32	The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.

If a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is wrong, fix the helper's Java, even if the prelude binds it, and leave the prelude's text: its binding gives the fix. 36	## What the compiled path cannot compile yet
37	
38	For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:
39	
40	- `spawn`;
41	- an object expression;
42	- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.
43	
44	It compiles a local function as a closure, also one that calls itself or another local function of its block. It refuses these forms (ledger row 304):
45	
46	- a local function with static parameters of its own: 'Can't compile a local function with static parameters of its own yet';
47	- two local functions of one name in a block: 'Can't compile overloaded local functions yet';
48	- a local function with the `atomic` modifier: 'Can't compile a local function with this modifier yet'.
49	
50	A type assumption `e asif T` has the value of `e`, but the call around it chooses its declaration as if `e` were a `T`, a supertype of `e`'s type (`Specification/basic/expressions/type-annotation.tex`). The code generator compiles one at a dotted call's receiver, at a call of a functional method or an overloaded function whose every argument is an assumption, and elsewhere as the value of `e`. It refuses these forms (ledger row 818):

52	- a call of a functional method or an overloaded function with an assumption at some of its arguments but not all: 'Can't compile a dispatched call whose arguments are not all type assumptions';
53	- a generic method on an assumed receiver: 'Can't compile a type assumption at the receiver of a generic method yet';
54	- a call of an overloaded generic function with an assumption at an argument: 'Can't compile a type assumption at a call of an overloaded generic function yet'.

It compiles a declaration whose own header or `extends` entry has a `where` clause, and emits nothing for the clause. It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private`, `abstract` and `test`, such as `override` (ledger row 650). A trait or object that extends a generic trait compiles with `Any` as the static argument. With `Bottom`, `Self` or an abbreviated type there, the code generator refuses the declaration. So a coercion's output comes before the program's first line, and the parallel parts of a coercion's body run one after another there. A coercion that raises stops the program before `run()`. 113	- An `atomic` block (`atomic do ... end`) or atomic expression (`atomic e`, as `atomic 1`), a `try` or a `label` block as a call's argument after the first, as `f(k, atomic do ... end)`, fails with a `VerifyError` at class load, unless the arguments fork (ledger row 322). So does a `try` as an operator's operand after the first (ledger row 526). Bind its value in a statement of its own.
114	- Numerals and sizes depart from `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways:
115	  - At a place whose type names a type parameter of its generic declaration, a numeral's coercion runs at each evaluation (ledger row 957). If the body needs the value at one instance only, bind it once, at a top-level variable whose type names no type parameter.
116	  - Until the switch-over, `RR64` converts only an `RR32` and a numeral, and `RR32` only a numeral. So a `ZZ32` value where an `RR64` is expected is refused (ledger row 442). Write `i.asRR64` for a `ZZ32` value `i`.
117	  - Where a variable without a declared type is bound to a block that ends in a numeral after a local declaration, the variable keeps the numeral's own type. A later conversion of such a variable `x`, as `y: ZZ32 = x`, dies at run time, with `NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerBuiltin$v` (ledger row 1060). Declare the variable's type.
118	  - A numeral with a radix point at a place that fixes no type, which rounds to an infinity at `RR64`, gives `Infinity`, as under walk (ledger row 980). Assert no value for it in a test.
119	  - A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, raises a `java.lang.Error` that no `catch` sees (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.
120	  - As a `typecase`'s selector, a numeral keeps its own type, as `NaturalNumeral[\1,10,7\]`, so `typecase 7 of ZZ32 => ...` is refused as unreachable (ledger row 963). Bind the selector to a variable first, as `x = 7`, then write `typecase x of ...`.
121	  - A `label` block that ends in a numeral, where an `exit ... with` gives the block a `ZZ32` value, stops the code generator: 'Error trying to close method scope' (ledger row 340). Bind the numeral to a typed variable first, as `none: ZZ32 = -1`, and end the block with the variable.
122	  - At a place that fixes a type (`revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"), the checker refuses an atomic expression whose value is a numeral, as `atomic if c then 1 else 0 end`, and `atomic 1` fails the JVM's verification (ledger row 1043). Write `atomic do ... end`.
123	- An `exit` that runs after its `label` block has completed, from a function made in the block, ends a compiled program with the Java exception `LabelExit`, which no `catch` clause takes. Under walk, a `catch` clause of the library's `LabelException` takes it. The rules do not settle which is right (ledger row 1041).
124	- Where an object overloads an inherited functional method by declarations of its own, and `self` is not the first parameter, the compiled dispatch method tests the receiver's type where it should test the other argument's. A call then dies with `ClassCastException` (ledger row 573). Where the receiver has the parameter type of one of the object's own declarations, the call runs that declaration whatever the argument (ledger row 1038). Put `self` first in such overloads.
125	- On the compiled path, two `value` objects with a `var` field, built alike, are not strictly equivalent: `V(1) === V(1)` is `false` (ledger row 112).
126	- A reference to a generic function with one declaration, as `count[\F extends Object\](b: Box[\F\]): ZZ32`, takes its instance from the arrow type that receives it. Where the receiving type is not an arrow type, as in `p(count)` for `p(x: Any)`, the compile passes and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError` (ledger row 1012). Write the static argument there, as `p(count[\ZZ32\])`. The checker refuses a reference to a name with several declarations of which one is generic, unless one without static parameters fits the receiving arrow type (ledger row 1009). Pass a function of one declaration that calls the name.
127	- Where the initialiser of a top-level variable `b` assigns to a top-level `var a`, a compiled read of `a` before the first read of `b` gives the old value (ledger row 1011). Read `b` before you read `a`.
128	- A `typecase` tuple pattern with an untyped binder, as `(x, y: ZZ32)`, stops the code generator: 'typcase match failure!' (ledger row 964). Give each binder a type.
129	- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
130	- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
131	- A clean link does not prove that every call has its method. These die at run time with `NoSuchMethodError`:
132	  - a call of a functional method of an object that a trait's `comprises` clause lists, on a value whose static type is the object. An example is `num(R)`, where `trait Q comprises { R }` declares `abstract num(self): ZZ32` and `object R extends Q` gives its body. Call it through a value typed as the trait, as `q: Q = R` and then `num(q)` (ledger row 815);
133	  - a read of an exported object's value parameter, from a component that imports the api, where the exporting component names the parameter otherwise than the api. A value parameter is a parameter of the object's constructor, and also a field. An example is `Np(3).a`, where the api declares `object Np(a: ZZ32)` and the component `object Np(z: ZZ32)`. The export check compares no value parameter's name. Give each value parameter the api's name (ledger row 839);
134	  - an assignment from outside an object to its `var` field, of a value whose static type is strictly below the field's type, as `c.t := High` for `trait T`, `object Cell(var t: T)` and `object High extends T`. Bind the value at the field's type first, as `h: T = High` (ledger row 1053).

136	## The checker's gaps
137	
138	- Overloads: in its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays. The paths differ on `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects. The checker refuses it, because `Box[\Bottom\]` lies in both domains, and walk loads it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 786).
139	- The Return Type Rule: the checker refuses a pair of declarations that the rule accepts: a generic declaration beside one without static parameters whose domain is a tuple of object types, as `ident[\T\](x: T): T` beside `ident(x: (Circle, Circle)): (Circle, Circle)`, `Circle` an object (ledger row 1048). Walk loads and runs the pair.
140	- A tie: where two generic candidates fit a call equally, the checker sorts the candidates and keeps the first. The sort's order varies with what the same JVM compiled before. So the call's static type, or a crash, 'V is not in the kind env', can change with the order of the suite (ledger rows 499, 1046, 1047). If a compiled test passes alone and fails in the suite, look for such a tie first.
141	- Inheritance: the checker refuses an object that reaches a generic self-typed trait's method along two paths, one through a trait that declares the method again at the same parameter types: 'There are multiple declarations of m with the same parameter type'. Without static parameters it accepts the form. Walk runs the lower trait's declaration. The specification's section "Method Declarations" (`Specification/basic/traits.tex`) does not settle which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 1037).
142	- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the compiled code does not check it. A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:
143	  - at a dotted call, a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable;
144	  - at a type's use, a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable;
145	  - a static argument written at a top-level call, against its parameter's bound (ledger row 470).
146	- A reduction without its static argument, whose bound names its parameter, such as `SUM`: the checker reports a type error in its body as the big operator's refusal, 'is not applicable to an argument of type ()' (ledger row 1015). Write the static argument to read the body's error.
147	- Imports: `import A.{...}`, with the three dots written, imports every name of `A`. The overloading check also reads `A`'s declarations of a name that the component imports by name from another api. So `import A.{...}` beside `import B.{ pick }`, where both apis declare `pick(x: P)`, is refused: 'There are multiple declarations of pick' (ledger row 813). Leave the name out of the whole import, as `import A.{...} except { pick }`.
148	- An `except` clause leaves out each identifier that it lists, on both paths. Neither path leaves out an infix operator that it lists. So where a component lists `-` in `except` and declares its own `-` at the api's parameter types, the code generator stops. Walk runs the component's own `-` (ledger row 814).
149	- Conditional extension: the condition holds while the checker checks the `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member. It does not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).
150	- A `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, as `NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]` or `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`: at a call, the checker gives the variable a fresh size or type, equal only to itself. Two values passed in one call get two. A fresh type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints. The variable is in scope in the trait, except in its `extends` and `excludes` clauses. The checker gives no fresh type where it meets the trait as a supertype of another type. Where a generic type that the clause lists, as `List[\E\]`, gives the body of a member of the trait, the code generator crashes: 'E is not in the kind env' (ledger row 812). Where the variable is a size, a compiled call that passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected fails the JVM's verification (ledger row 307). Departures: a fresh type also under a function type's result (ledger row 751), none for an extender that the clause does not list (ledger row 752), and a crash at a call, from outside the trait, of a member whose type names the variable (ledger row 756).

200	## The checker's time
201	
202	This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.
203	
204	The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 80 to 180 seconds, more under load. It can run past the Bash tool's 120-second limit, so run it in the background (`session.md`). It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.
205	
206	The checker checks every api first, and the component only if no api has an error. In each api or component, it stops at the first of its stages that finds errors. The stages run in this order (`compiler/StaticChecker.java`, `checkCompilationUnit`):
207	
208	1. The type hierarchy and the type check.
209	2. The overloading check, which also compares the overloads' return types.
210	3. In the component only, the export check (`library.md`, "Designing a change").
211	
212	So the count misses the errors of the later stages, and a fix of an early error can raise it.
213	
214	The table's rows tell a clean run from a run that the checker did not finish:
215	
216	- `#total 0` and `#locations 0`: the checker reached the component and found no error.
217	- `#stopped`, in place of `#total` and `#locations`: the errors came from a phase before the checker, such as the parse. The checker reported none and did not reach the component. The script exits 1, and the gate reads the table as red.
218	- `#crash`: the first crash of the overloading check that the run survived, or `none`.
219	
220	If the run printed no error total and was not clean, the script writes no table and exits 1.
221	
222	The checker's results are the programs that it accepts and refuses, and each error with its text and its place. On the interpreter's library, a change keeps the results the same if both of these hold:
223	
224	- The two tables are equal: `diff` prints nothing.
225	- The two `run.txt` files are equal after you replace each run's own tree path with one word, such as `TREE`. Any difference fails.
226	
227	A node's hash starts from its class name, so an order in the output, such as the apis' checks, does not vary from run to run. A moved order is a difference: keep the old order, or report it.
228	
229	`Walker`, in the generated `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, is split into methods under 8,000 bytes of bytecode. HotSpot does not compile a longer method, and the walker runs on every node. `MethodSizeJUTest` fails if a method of the build grows past the limit, except the methods that its source lists in `listed(...)` entries. Run it alone with `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=MethodSizeJUTest`. If a method of `Walker` fails, lower `WALKER_CASES_PER_METHOD` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/ScalaAstGenerator.java`. If another method fails, split it under the limit. List it only if nothing in the checker or a compiled run calls it, with its size and what runs it, and name it in your report.
230	
231	The timing is a smoke test, to catch a slowdown of several times. One run of each tree is enough. A small difference, or one within the noise from run to run, is not a finding. In your report, say what you saw, and do not analyse it.
232	
233	If you change the checker:
234	
235	1. Make the change correct, with its tests. Commit it, and name the commit in your report.
236	2. Time the base build and the change, named `base` and `change`. Run the base in a call set up for the base build (`build-and-caches.md`), and the change in a call set up for your tree, each in the background (`session.md`). Use the same command for both, with `N` the run's name:
237	
238	       export W=<your tree> N=base ; mkdir -p $W/tmp/count
239	       time explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh $W/tmp/count/$N.txt $W/tmp/count/$N
240	
241	3. Make a second pass that makes the checker faster. Start with a profile (below). Where the profile shows a gain, take it. Where it shows none, say so in your report, with the profile's top frames.
242	4. If the second pass changed code, run the count stage once more with the command of step 2, named `pass`. Show that its results are the same as `change`'s. Then run `ant testQuick` once more (`tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite"). If it changed nothing, run neither, and report `change`'s results in place of `pass`'s.
243	5. If the pass reuses an answer that the checker computed earlier, as a memo does, audit it on one full run. Put the audit in an instrumented copy ("Testing an edit here"), never in the tree. In the audit, compute each reused answer again and compare the two. If any answer differs, the reuse is wrong: fix it or drop it, then repeat step 4. Report the count of reuses and of differences.
244	6. In your report, give each run's seconds, the diff of the `base` and `change` tables, the comparison of their `run.txt` files, and that `pass` has the same results as `change`.

246	To find where the time goes, use JFR on the count stage's checker, instrumented copies compiled into a scratch folder ahead of the build on the class path, and the methods over 8,000 bytes that `MethodSizeJUTest` lists in its source. A profiled or instrumented run is neither a timed run nor a run to compare. Print the commands of two earlier speed probes (about 8 KB):

Time the base build and the worker's commit of step 1 once each, as step 2 says, with the commit and the worker's head in worktrees seeded at them (`worktrees.md`). Check that your times are the worker's, in order of size. Check that the commit's and the head's results are the same.

33	
34	A build, and a run of `bin/fortress` without a private caches folder, walk's too, write into the caches of the tree that they run in. So build and run only in a tree whose caches no other agent uses. Your brief says where you work. If your work builds or runs code and your brief gives you no tree of your own, seed a worktree of your own instead of building one. Then work only there.

36	Seeding takes about 3 s and 206 MB of disk. The new worktree runs walk and the compiled path right away, with the library already compiled.

38	    explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-build> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]
39	
40	- The script checks out `<branch>`: a local branch, else origin's, else a new branch cut from `<start-point>`, by default the base build's commit. With `-`, it makes a detached worktree at `<start-point>`.
41	- If the script exits 2, the base build is not built or not clean, and the script made nothing. Then make the worktree with `git worktree add`, build it yourself, and say so in your report.

49	## Running the old code
50	
51	If your worktree holds an edit and you need the base's behaviour, run the old code instead of reverting your edit. For example, see a test fail, or compare a program's old and new output.
52	
53	`old-fortress.sh` runs the base build's `bin/fortress`. It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the base build and `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the private caches folder that you name, over your settings. Name a folder inside your worktree's `tmp/`:
54	
55	    OLD=explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh
56	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss     # the compiled path ...
57	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P             # ... then the run
58	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss             # walk
59	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches junit <worktree>/ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/X.test [Y.test ...]   # compiled .test files, in one JVM
60	
61	- Any copy of the tool works, because it runs the base build that its first argument names.
62	- On first use, it fills the private folder with a copy of the base build's caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). Later runs use the same folder.
63	- Every cache file that a run writes goes to the private folder, and nothing else that it writes under the base build stays. So several agents can run the old code at once.
64	- Keep your programs outside the base build too, because a program writes its own logs beside it. The tool refuses a private folder inside the base build (exit 2).

66	To run interpreter tests on the old code, run the base build's `harness-one.sh` with `FORTRESS_HOME` set to the base build:
67	
68	    FORTRESS_HOME=<base-build> <base-build>/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh \
69	        <worktree>/tmp/old-harness <worktree>/ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss
70	
71	The `run` step of a compiled `.test` is a separate `bin/fortress run` process. It inherits `FORTRESS_HOME` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`, and takes its class path from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. If you compose a harness run by hand with `-Dfortress.caches=<folder>`, set `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the same folder. Otherwise the `run` step fails with "Could not load ... Resource not found".
