# Review of the array design for the compiled world

## 0. What was checked and how

The design's own citations were opened: every line number in §1, §2, §4c, §5, §6a-§6e and §8 was read in the tree, and the two rulings were read in `POSITIONS.md:40`. Where the design says "unprobed" or "not measured", or where a claim depends on what the checker does rather than on what the interpreter does, a probe was run: five Fortress programs through `fortress compile` under a private cache (one also through the interpreter), and two Java models beside the kernel models of `perf-probes/kernels/java`. Nothing under `default_repository/`, `Library/` or `ProjectFortress/` was touched.

The standard applied is the one in the brief: finish what the designers intended, judged by the July 2012 draft and the breadcrumbs in all three sources of truth (specification, interpreter and its library, compiler and its prelude); storage is `double[]`, unboxed; sizes are `nat` parameters and the two forks are taken together; extensions go into the standard library in the library's own patterns; and the measuring stick is one program, microGPT compiled and running fast.

### Serious 4. "Natives first" contradicts the ruling's letter, has no team precedent, and is measured to deliver nothing on the shapes the model is made of

What the design says. §7 question 3, default: "natives first, with the kernel measurement in the first array rung; generated-code unboxing as PLAN's step 4"; §4b admits "Without it, an unboxed store with boxed traffic is what `ZZ32Vector` is today; whether that alone is faster than boxed storage is not measured".

Measured now (`compiler-probes/array-design-review/java-medians.tsv`, the kernels' harness, medians of 3). Unboxed `double[]` storage read and written through a boxing accessor, arithmetic boxed as the runtime boxes it: `kdot` 0.007559 s, 8.9× primitive, against boxed storage 0.005495 s (6.4×) and primitive 0.000852 s; `kmat` 0.005552 s, 6.6×, against boxed 0.005255 s (6.2×) and primitive 0.000844 s. The store buys nothing until the traffic is unboxed; the design's §2 already showed the traffic on `ZZ32Vector` is four calls and an allocation per element (probe 2).

Where the model's traffic is. The model's data design is views: nine `PView`s over the flat vector, `RowView`, `Row3View`, `heads`, `unheads`, `plane`, `Diag`, `Transposed3` (`FlatArrays.fss:40-120`), each a `get` that indexes another array. A native product over a view reads its operand through `get`, boxed; a native `dot` over the store helps `p DOT p` and Adam's three lines (`MicroGptFlat.fss:76-79`) and nothing in `step`. So the first rung's number (`kdot` over a store) would not transfer to the program the number is for.

Precedent. The team's compiler-world operators over `ZZ32Vector` are Fortress `for` loops over boxed subscripts (`CompilerLibrary.fss:484-535`), and the team's unboxing note is a code-generator taxonomy (`Unbox.java`); the design says of natives "Not the team's precedent" (§4b) and defaults to them anyway. The route with the precedent, and the only one under which "it cannot be boxed" is true of the model, is unboxing by static type in generated code (roadmap A1, `Unbox.java` case 1), which is the largest code-generator work in the plan. Decision B.

### Minor 11. What the specification's own breadcrumb on unboxed arrays says, which the design does not cite

Jan's note #82 on unboxed types (`appendices/future.tex:42`): "Do we want to permit arrays of fixed bounds to be unboxed? No. Unboxed arrays are a different other thing. Among other things, an array of fixed bounds may be a segment of another array." That is the team saying that a sized array is a structure (possibly a view) over a linear store and that the store is the thing to unbox, which is the shape of option (c) and of `HeapSequence` (`arrays-distributed.tex:18-22`). It supports the design's separation of sized traits from a native store; it should be in §5.

## 3. Decisions that are Pavol's

Each as what we do, what it changes, the alternatives, and a labelled default that can be accepted without reading the argument; the argument is in §1.

### Decision A. What puts `double[]` under the library's sized traits

What we do: choose the mechanism by which `Vector[\RR64,16\]` gets a `double[]` store while `Vector[\T,16\]` for other `T` gets a boxed one.

What it changes: which `.java` rung the array work needs first, and whether the library's generic factories keep their text.

Alternatives. (A1) The design's default, a factory selecting by run-time type tag under one generic storing object: refused by the checker (finding 2); to keep it, a code-generator special case for the factory, a `.java` rung with no team precedent. (A2) The team's direction: the code generator and loader give a stamped `PrimitiveArray⟦FRR64,n⟧` a `double[]` field, `Unbox.java` case 1 plus the expando stub; the library's text stays as it is; the largest change, in the loader and `CodeGen`, and `PLAN.md` step 5's own first probe. (A3) Monomorphic storing objects per native element type (`__RR64Vector[\nat s0\]`) beside the generic boxed one, with a monomorphic factory name per element type in the manner of `array1`/`vector` (`.fss:2251`); typed cleanly, no code-generator change, but the model then names `rr64vector`, not `vector`, and the generic `Vector[\T,s0\]` is boxed for every `T` including `RR64` unless the user calls the right factory.

Default: probe A2 first (one shadow experiment, `next-climb.md` §3b's first item), because it is the team's breadcrumb and `PLAN.md`'s order; A3 is the fallback that needs no `.java`; A1 is closed by the probe unless Pavol wants the special case.

### Decision B. Where loops run unboxed

What we do: choose between Java natives per whole-array operation and unboxing `RR64` by static type in generated code.

What it changes: whether the ruling "it cannot be boxed" holds for the model (views, lambdas, `rows`) or only for whole-array operations on stores; and the size of the code-generator work.

Alternatives. (B1) Natives first, the design's default: measured at 8.9×/6.6× primitive on the model's shapes (finding 4), the same as boxed storage; helps `p DOT p` and Adam only; no precedent. (B2) Unboxing by static type first (roadmap A1, `Unbox.java` case 1): `D` locals, `daload`/`dastore`, `dadd`/`dmul` wherever the checker's type is `RR64`; the library's own Fortress loops (`fill`, `map`, `Vector.dot`) become unboxed without natives; every rung `.java` under the full gate; the team's precedent. (B3) Both, in the order B2 for element access and arithmetic, natives only where a whole-array kernel beats the JIT (a measured residue, not a default).

Default: B2, because it is the only alternative under which the ruling is true of the model, and the kernel measurement in the array rung is then `kdot` in Fortress against `KDotPrim`, not against a native.

content.content:
## The answer in short

- A carrier is the JVM class whose instances are the values of a built-in type at run time. Today `FZZ32`, a class written by hand in Java, carries the prelude's `ZZ32`.
- The two libraries declare a built-in type in two shapes. The prelude says `trait ZZ32`, and `FZZ32` is the trait's class. The interpreter's library says `trait ZZ32 comprises { Int }` with `value object Int extends ZZ32`, and `value object Boolean` with no trait at all.
- I found nine ways. Four give the type its class (A to D). Three are ruled out (E, F, G). Two are later layers for speed, not carriers (H, I).
- The four that count:
  - **A.** The trait's class is written by hand, and the objects leave the library. This is the prelude's way, whole.
  - **B.** The trait's class is written by hand, and an empty object stands below each trait. This is the rehearsal's hack.
  - **C.** The object's class carries the value. The trait stays a plain interface. The library's text does not change. This is walk's own way, brought to the compiled path.
  - **D.** One object per type: each number trait is merged with its one object, as `NN32`, `RR32`, `Boolean` and `Char` already are. Then C's machinery, with one name per type.
- The team's later word, the library as the team wrote it, and the peers do not point to one way. The library as written points to C. The peers point to D. The team's later code is A's shape, but its author called it a special case "for the time being", and its own plan for unboxing is written over objects and `comprises` clauses, which is C's and D's shape.
- I recommend C now, and D as a second step that the curator rules on apart. C changes no line of the library, keeps walk as it is, removes W13 and W14 by construction, and closes the hole of ledger row 866. It gives up the prelude's trick of one hand-written class per type with no change in the code generator: the code generator must learn that a native object has a payload.

## The words

- **Built-in type.** A type whose values the language's implementation makes, not a constructor call: the numbers, `Boolean`, `Char`, the flat string, and a few Java-backed values (a reader, a writer, an array's store).
- **Carrier.** The JVM class of a built-in type's values on the compiled path.
- **Payload.** The Java value inside a carrier: an `int` in `FZZ32`, a `double` in `FRR64`, a `java.lang.String` in `FJavaString`.
- **Box.** A carrier object on the heap. A number is unboxed where the compiled code holds the payload itself: a JVM `double` in a local, a field or an array.
- **Springboard.** The class `T$DefaultTraitMethods` that the code generator writes for a trait `T`. It holds the trait's method bodies. An object's class extends the springboard of the first trait that the object extends (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:888-909`).
- **Stub.** A Java source file that declares, empty, the classes that the code generator will write, so that hand-written Java can extend them before any Fortress is compiled: `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/CompilerBuiltin.java`.
- **Closed type.** A type that no program can extend: an object, or a trait whose `comprises` clause lists its only subtypes. An open type is a trait without such a clause.
- **Native component.** A component declared `native component`. The specification says that inside one "the syntax and semantics are implementation dependent" (`Specification/basic/components/source-code.tex:513-518`). The library's four are `FortressBuiltin`, `FlatString`, `Reflect` and `AnyType`.

## What stands today

### The prelude: a trait, and a class written by hand

    trait ZZ32 extends { Number, Equality[\ZZ32\], StandardTotalOrder[\ZZ32\] }
            excludes { ZZ64, RR32, RR64 }
        opr +(self, other:ZZ32): ZZ32 = jIntOverflowingAdd(self,other)
        ...
    end

(`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:662`.) Beside it, in Java:

    public final class FZZ32 extends fortress.CompilerBuiltin.ZZ32.DefaultTraitMethods
            implements fortress.CompilerBuiltin.ZZ32 {
        final int val;
        public int getValue() {return val;}
        public static FZZ32 make(int x) { return new FZZ32(x); }
        public RTTI getRTTI() { return RTTIc.ONLY; }
    }

(`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32.java:14-43`.)

- The code generator writes the interface `fortress/CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32` and its springboard from the trait.
- `FZZ32` extends that springboard. So the Java build needs the stub file.
- A table says that the type `ZZ32` is written `FZZ32` in every descriptor: `compiler/NamingCzar.java:587-601`, and a copy for the run in `runtimeSystem/Naming.java:294-306`.
- The class of `Box[\ZZ32\]` is named with the carrier: `Box⟦com|sun|fortress|compiler|runtimeValues|FZZ32⟧` (`runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java:56`).
- Fifteen names are carried so: `Boolean`, `Character`, `ZZ`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ32`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `RR32`, `RR64`, `JavaString`, `JavaBufferedReader`, `JavaBufferedWriter`, `ZZ32Vector`, `StringVector` and `()`.

The prelude's trait is open. A program may write `object MyNum extends ZZ32`. The checker takes it, the compile exits 0, and the run dies: 'IncompatibleClassChangeError: class OpenZ$MyInt can not implement com.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ32, because it is not an interface'. Ledger row 866 holds this. I ran it again today (section "The probe").

content.content:
### Way C. The object's class carries the value, and the trait stays an interface

This is walk's way, brought to the compiled path. The library's text does not change.

**On `ZZ32`.** The declarations stay as they are today. The code generator compiles them as it compiles any trait and object, with one addition for a native object:

    interface fortress/FortressLibrary$ZZ32                      (from trait ZZ32)
    final class fortress/FortressBuiltin$Int implements ...$ZZ32 (from value object Int)
        final int val;
        static Int make(int)        int getValue()

- The carrier is `Int`'s class. It has `asFloat`'s body, because `Int` declares it. So W13 does not arise.
- `Int extends ZZ32` names the interface, as every `extends` clause does. Nothing extends a carrier, because nothing extends an object. So W14 does not arise.
- A table gives each native object its payload: `Int` an `int`, `Float` a `double`, `FlatString` a `java.lang.String`, `BigNum` a `BigInteger`. This is the table of `NamingCzar` today, keyed by the object.
- One rule answers W12: a value of a native object is read at its trait where a static argument is formed, and the stamped class is named by the carrier. Walk has this rule (F-344). The checker already lets a value of `trait T comprises { O }` stand where `O` is expected (the rehearsal's W7).
- A value of static type `ZZ32` is exactly an `Int`, because the trait says `comprises { Int }`. So a descriptor for `ZZ32` may name `Int`'s class, as a descriptor names `FZZ32` today. The cast that row 307 asks for is the same knowledge.

**On `Boolean`.** `value object Boolean` compiles to its own class, with a `boolean` payload. Its methods written in Fortress (`cond`, `generate`, `=`) are the object's methods. No trait, no second name.

**On `String`.** `String` is an interface. `FlatString`'s class holds a `java.lang.String`. `CatString`, `EmptyString` and `SubString` are plain classes. A helper's Java `String` result becomes a `FlatString` value. The wrapper generator reads a helper's Java `String` parameter as the trait `String` (`NamingCzar.java:484`), so the wrapper casts it to `FlatString`'s class: the rehearsal's new converter. The cast is safe because the library's bindings pass a `FlatString` there: walk refuses a helper parameter declared `String` other than `self` (the skill's `references/interpreter.md`, "Natives"). The table could read such a parameter as `FlatString` instead. This is the same in every way.

**On `Float`.** `Float`'s class holds a `double` and has its 146 lines as its own methods. `RR64` is an interface. A call `x + y` on two `RR64` values dispatches to `Float`'s `+`, as under walk.

**Where the class comes from: three forms.** This choice is inside way C.

1. Written by hand, extending the object's generated springboard, as `FZZ32` extends the trait's today. It needs the stub files, and `FlatString` cannot be stubbed in Java (the rehearsal's W2: Java allows no class `FlatString` nested in a class `FlatString`).
2. Written by the code generator, over a small payload class written by hand: `abstract class FZZ32 extends FValue { final int val; getValue() }`, and the generated `Int extends FZZ32`. No stub is needed, because the hand-written class extends nothing generated. The run time's Java keeps a name to test, as `nativeHelpers/equalityRule.java:38` tests `instanceof FZZ32`. The object then takes its traits' default methods by forwarding methods, which the code generator already writes for every trait after the first (`CodeGen.java:888-909`).
3. Written whole by the code generator, with the payload as a hidden field. The run time's Java then reaches the payload through a small interface.

Form 2 looks best to me: no stubs, and the box's chain of constructors is three classes, `Int`, `FZZ32`, `FValue`. Today's chain through the one library's springboards is six, which leaves a margin of two frames before HotSpot stops removing temporary boxes (F-302). Not measured.

**What blocks it.** The code generator compiles an object without value parameters as a singleton, one instance. A native object has many values. The specification leaves a native component's meaning to the implementation, and walk uses that freedom in the same place. So the block is in the code generator only, and it gets around it as walk does: by the component's `native` mark and a table.

**What it changes.**

- The library's text: nothing. (`NN32`'s `zero` and `one`, the rehearsal's W4, are a defect apart.)
- Walk: nothing.
- The code generator: a native object gets a payload, `make` and `getValue`, and many instances; the tables are keyed by the object; a trait with one comprised native object is named by that object's class in descriptors; the wrapper generator's converters read the same table. About three rungs, the rehearsal's own estimate for W2's repair, with W12's rule among them.
- The run-time classes: the thirteen become payload classes (form 2) or are re-parented (form 1). `equalityRule`, `FValue.asString`, `Utility` and `FException` name the new classes. The helpers' 99 raise strings change in every way.
- The loader: the run's copy of the table (`Naming.java`), and one canonical name for a stamp.
- The tests: the compiled tests stay. New tests: `typecase x of Int`, `Box(3)` as a `Box[\ZZ32\]` compiled, a program's `object MyNum extends ZZ32` refused by the checker (row 866's test promoted).

**Speed later.** It helps.

- The type is closed in the language itself. So "a value of static type `RR64` is a `double`" is sound, and the code generator can choose unboxed arithmetic by static type (PLAN's phase 6, decision B; P-17).
- In a field: a field declared `RR64` in a plain object can become a `double` field. A field of type `T` in `Box[\T\]` needs the loader to stamp a different class (F-18); the canonical name of W12's rule is what it would key on.
- In an array: the store is already a `double[]` (`JavaRR64ArrayStore`, F-333; P-84). The carrier decides only which box `get` returns until phase 6.
- Across a call: a function `f(x: RR64): RR64` can take the descriptor `(D)D`, because no other class can arrive.
- Dispatch on a built-in type tests one final class, as today. With the closed type, the test can be dropped where the static type is the trait.
- The team's bytecode optimizer finds a box by the methods `make` and `getValue` on a carried type (`compiler/asmbytecodeoptimizer/MethodInsn.java:71-85`). Way C keeps both names.

**Undo.** Cheap. The library and walk are untouched. Going to way D later is additive. Going to way A later costs what way A costs today.

**The team's texts.** For: the interpreter's library as written; walk's native components; the specification's value objects and its `trait Boolean ... comprises { ... }`; Chase's unboxing plan of 2009, whose cases are objects and `comprises`. Against: the prelude and its run time put the class on the trait.

### Way D. One object per type: each number trait merged with its one object

This is the library's own way for `NN32`, `RR32`, `Boolean` and `Char`, applied to the five number traits. It is way C plus one change of the library's text.

**On `ZZ32`.**

    value object ZZ32 extends { AnyIntegral, Integral[\ZZ32\], Index }
        coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) = v.asZZ32
        asFloat(self): RR64 = builtinPrimitive("...simpleIntArith.intToDouble")
        opr =(self, b:ZZ32):Boolean = builtinPrimitive("...simpleIntArith.intEQ")
        ...
    end

`Int` is gone. The `excludes` and `comprises` clauses go too: an object excludes every type that it does not extend. The class:

    final class ZZ32 { final int val; ... }     (one declaration, one class, one name)

**On `Boolean`.** Nothing changes: it is already this shape. The same for `Char`, `NN32`, `RR32`.

**On `String`.** Nothing changes: `String` has four objects, so it stays a trait, as in way C.

**On `Float`.** `value object RR64` takes `Float`'s 146 lines. About 50 bodies of `trait RR64` go: `opr +(self,b:RR64):RR64 = asFloat(self) + asFloat(b)` and its like (`FortressLibrary.fss:408-504`; 57 lines of the trait hold `asFloat(self)`). They served when `RR64` had four subtypes. Today every `RR64` is a `Float`, so `Float`'s own `+` is always the more specific one, and by the dispatch rule these bodies never run. By reading; no test shows it.

**Why the split is there.** It was made for two reasons, and both are gone.

- Maessen split `ZZ32` on 2008-07-15 so that `IntLiteral` could be a subtype of `ZZ32` (`fca589bbb0`: "ZZ32 is now a trait, with subtypes Int and IntLiteral"). The numerals have their own types now (P-173, P-174), and `IntLiteral` left the library.
- The other traits had subtypes by nesting: `trait ZZ64 ... comprises { Long, ZZ32 }` at the team's last commit. The tower is flat now (P-43).

So each of the five traits has exactly one object, and the split serves nothing that the record names.

**What blocks it.** Under walk, an object with native values must be in a native component. `FortressLibrary` is not one. So the five move into `FortressBuiltin`, beside `NN32` and `RR32`, or walk learns one more place. The names `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong` go: by a grep of whole words, the library names them on 4, 4, 41, 4 and 4 lines, almost all in their own declarations. A few tests name one as a type, among them `tests/NumberPrintTest.fss:31-35`, `tests/NativeHelperFloatCarriedWalk.fss:5-6` and `compiler_tests/XXXNativeHelperOwnUnsignedLongCompiled.fss:8`. No model line does.

**What it changes.**

- The library's text: five objects deleted, five traits made objects and moved, about 600 lines moved, about 50 dead bodies deleted.
- Walk: five constructor classes renamed; the reading of F-344 and the ilk names of F-328 become needless for the numbers and stay for the strings.
- The code generator: as way C, without the rule for a trait with one comprised object, and without W12's rule for the numbers.
- The run-time classes and the loader: as way C.
- The tests: `tests/LanguageTypeInstancesWalk` and `tests/FlatTowerRungF` change where they name the objects. The checker's count and the distance are run again. I did not run them: this is the first probe to make before the way is chosen.

**Speed later.** As way C, and a little more: one declaration per operator instead of two, so the dispatch method of `+` has one arm less for each number type, and the static type is the class with no rule in between.

**Undo.** The merge is mechanical each way, but it changes text that the team wrote. From C, it can be taken at any time. From D back to C, the objects are written again.

**The team's texts.** For: `NN32` (Steele, 2008), `RR32` (Ryu, 2008), `Boolean` and `Char` are this shape in the library; the prelude's first number types were objects (Flood, 2009-03-03); the library's own complaint about `Float` against `RR64` (below); every peer. Against: the specification's api style shows a built-in type as a trait with hidden comprised types; the split is the team's text, though its reasons are gone.

### Way E. The payload written in the library's text

    value object Int(v: JavaInt32) extends ZZ32
        asFloat(self): RR64 = intToDouble(self.v)
    end

The object is plain Fortress, and its one field has a Java-backed type. The code generator writes the class as for any object. The library does this for `Ratio(num: ZZ, den: ZZ)`, for the I/O objects over `JavaBufferedWriter` (P-164) and for the arrays over `JavaArrayStore` (F-333).

**What blocks it.** It does not end. `JavaInt32` is itself a built-in type that needs a carrier, by one of the other ways. The language has no type for a Java `int`: the specification lists a foreign-function interface among the things to do (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:706-710`; P-58), and the prelude's `import java` reads a Java `int` back as `ZZ32` itself (`NamingCzar.java:439-440`). So way E adds a second box around the first. That hinders speed until fields are unboxed.

It is the right way for a type made of other types, and the library already uses it there. It is not a way for the numbers.

### Way F. The JDK's own classes as carriers

`ZZ32` is `java.lang.Integer`, `String` is `java.lang.String`, as Kotlin does for a boxed `Int`.

**What blocks it.** Every Fortress value implements the interface `fortress/AnyType$Any` and answers `getRTTI()` (`compiler/runtimeValues/FValue.java:14-19`). A JDK class cannot implement an interface of ours. The team wraps instead: 'because we know these types are already loaded and not eligible for ASM-wrapping' (`NamingCzar.java:416-418`). To get around it, `Any` would be erased to `java.lang.Object` and the type of a value found from its class. The team's paper names that erasure only for union types (`Papers/Implementation/TypeMapping.tex:177`). It would change dispatch, RTTI and every descriptor. Ruled out by cost.

### Way G. The prelude's built-in types kept as a compiled-only component

The compiled path keeps a small `CompilerBuiltin` with the carried traits, and the one library's `ZZ32` is an alias of it.

**What blocks it.** P-37 deletes the prelude's three files. A `type` alias stops its component on both paths (row 18). And walk would read another text than the compiled path. Ruled out.

### Way H. No class: a JVM primitive, chosen by static type

A local of type `RR64` is a JVM `double`; `f(x: RR64): RR64` is `(D)D`; the box is made only where the value meets `Any`, a trait above it or a type parameter. Scala and Kotlin do this.

This is not a carrier. It is the layer that P-17 requires and that PLAN's phase 6 names as decision B. A box class is still needed, and ways A to D say which. The team planned this layer: Chase's `Unbox.java` (below), and the six names of `NamingCzar.java:262-281`, of which the third is "I, the signature encoding of Java int". It needs the type closed: ways C and D give that by the language, way B by its empty object, way A not at all.

### Way I. Classes specialised by the loader

`Box⟦RR64⟧` gets a `double` field, where today the loader only renames `T` to `FRR64` (F-18). The loader's stub for it is empty: '// Here will go all the magic expando-stuff.' (`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`). C# does this.

Also a later layer, not a carrier: way A4 of the array decision (P-85). It keys on the name of the static argument in a stamp, so it needs W12 answered, which every way must do.

## 2. For the curator

### The words this record uses

- **Walk** is the interpreter. The **compiled path** first checks a program's types with the **checker**, then writes JVM bytecode with the **code generator**.
- The **prelude** is the small library that the compiled path uses today. The **one library** is the interpreter's library. The **switch-over** is the move of the compiled path onto the one library, after which the prelude is deleted.
- Your decision P-33 says how the switch-over's work goes: first microGPT's **slice**, the parts of the one library that microGPT needs. The **selector** lets one compile command read the one library beside the prelude. Each problem that only the one library shows is then fixed as its own small change, with its own test, under the full check.
- A **wall** is a place where the compiler or the compiled library stops.
- A **rung** is one change. One worker builds it, and a second, the skeptic, checks it. A **run** is one launch of the batch workflow. The **gate** is the full check before a run lands.
- A **value object** is an object without identity: two with equal contents are the same value. No type can extend an object.
- A **payload class** is a small class written by hand in Java that holds a bare JVM `int`, `long` or `double`. Under the chosen form, the code generator writes the class of `ZZ32` itself, on top of the payload class `FZZ32`.
- The **ledger** is the list of known defects. A **row** is one defect. An **expected-failure test** is a test that is known to fail and is marked so.
- **microGPT** is the model program. No rung changes a line of it.

### The go

None yet. You asked on 13 November for this batch to be planned, and said that its start is not authorized. The coordinator launches nothing until you say so. Each fork below has a default. None needs your answer before the start: none bends a decision of yours, and none touches microGPT.

### The two runs

- **Run 1, climb batch 33, six rungs:** S, D, V, Q, I and C.
- **Run 2, climb batch 33b, four rungs:** N, W, G and R, on run 1's landed tree.
- **Why two runs.** N, W, G and R need S on `main` first. N's table of names follows S's selector, and the tests of W, G and R compile programs under it. A rung cannot build on another rung of its own run.
- **Why I is in run 1.** Rung N of run 2 edits the same method of the code generator. In run 1 no rung edits it.

### Run 1, rung by rung

<!-- A rehearsal of the switch-over by brute force, 2026-11-10, by a Fable worker for the review of PLAN's phases 4 and 5: a scratch tree's compiled path switched onto the interpreter's library, the library's components compiled to bytecode with every wall hacked past, and programs run against them, with each wall in the order met, its ledger row or the lack of one, the hack that passed it and what a real repair needs; run in a worktree of the worker's own, `/home/user/fortress-switch`, seeded from the base build `/home/user/fortress-base32` (`832f7d0d91`) and removed after; nothing here lands, and the scratch tree's whole diff is `switch-rehearsal.patch` beside this report. -->

# The switch-over rehearsed by brute force

The question: what stands between today's tree (`832f7d0d91`) and a program that compiles to bytecode and runs against the interpreter's library (P-37, P-33)? The method: switch a scratch tree's compiled path onto that library by the smallest change, then push, hacking past each wall, and record the walls in the order met. A hack is marked as one in the patch (`SWITCH HACK`), and the patch is not a design.

Machine: nproc 4, Intel Xeon Processor @ 2.30GHz, OpenJDK 25, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`. Other sessions share the machine.

How the runs were made: the edited Java and Scala classes compiled into a scratch folder put first on the class path (the `fortress-repo` skill's `compiler.md`, "Testing an edit here"), with a private caches folder that started empty; one `ant compileAll` after the run-time classes changed.

## 1. The switch itself

The two worlds are chosen in one place for each command: `Shell.useCompilerLibraries()` and `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java:373-388`), which point `WellKnownNames` and `Types` at a prelude and set the desugaring switches. The smallest change that switches the compiled path is two lines of `useCompilerLibraries()`:

    -        WellKnownNames.useCompilerLibraries();
    -        Types.useCompilerLibraries();
    +        WellKnownNames.useFortressLibraries();
    +        Types.useFortressLibraries();

The desugaring switches stay the compile command's. With that alone, `fortress compile Hello.fss` (one `println` of a string) passes every phase, the checker and the code generator among them, in 16 s, and writes `Hello.jar`. The program's own compile needs nothing else. Everything below is what its run needs: the library as bytecode.

## 2. The walls, in the order met

Each wall has: what fails, its kind and count, the ledger row that holds it or "no row", the hack, and what a real repair needs.

### W1. No jar of the library exists (the run)

`fortress run Hello`:

    Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/FortressLibrary$String
    Caused by: java.io.IOException: Resource not found : fortress/FortressLibrary$String.class

Nothing compiles the library's components for a program: each must be compiled by name, as the library order does for the prelude today. Not a defect; the switch-over's library order is fourteen compiles (section 4) in place of five. No row; the plan's names line does not state the new library order.

### W2. The wrappers of the helper classes (row 874)

`fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss`:

    java.lang.RuntimeException: Can't generate header for method floatToString with jvm desc =Ljava/lang/String; stripped = FortressLibrary$String

Row 874 holds it, as PLAN's N5 says. It is not one table but the question of which run-time class carries each of the one library's built-in types on the compiled path. The record does not hold that design; PLAN names only `FlatString`'s carrier as unmeasured. What the hack had to decide (all of it `SWITCH HACK`):

- `NamingCzar`'s table of types that a hand-written class carries, and `Naming`'s copy of it for the run: `FortressLibrary`'s `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `RR64`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `JavaBufferedReader`, `JavaBufferedWriter` to `FZZ32`, `FZZ64`, `FRR64`, `FNN64`, `FZZ`, `FJavaBufferedReader`, `FJavaBufferedWriter`; `FortressBuiltin`'s `Boolean`, `RR32`, `NN32`, `Char` to `FBoolean`, `FRR32`, `FNN32`, `FCharacter`; `FlatString`'s `FlatString` to `FJavaString`.
- The wrapper generator's converters (`FortressMethodAdapter`): a helper's Java `String` is read as the trait `String`, which no class carries (a `CatString` is a `String` too), so the wrapper takes the trait's interface and casts to `FJavaString`; a new converter. A helper's Java `Object` at `Any` had no converter either ('stripped = AnyType$Any', met at `arrayOps.get`); a second new converter.
- The array stores (met as its own failure, 'Can't generate header for method make with jvm desc =Lcom/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FortressArrayStore; stripped = FortressLibrary$JavaArrayStore'): `FortressArrayStore` and `FortressRR64ArrayStore` are plain Java classes outside the Fortress hierarchy, so `JavaArrayStore` and `JavaRR64ArrayStore` have no compiled value. Two new run-time classes, `FJavaArrayStore` and `FJavaRR64ArrayStore`, each a store in a field. F-333 says the stores are built; they are, but nothing carries one as a Fortress value on the compiled path.
- The run-time classes extend the prelude's generated classes by name in their Java source (`FZZ32 extends fortress.CompilerBuiltin.ZZ32.DefaultTraitMethods`), against bootstrap stubs in `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/CompilerBuiltin.java`. Thirteen classes re-parented onto the one library's traits, with new stubs `fortress/FortressLibrary.java`, `FortressBuiltin.java` and `FlatStringC.java`; `FValue.asString` and `Utility.makeFortressException` name the one library's `String`; the helpers' 99 raise strings name `fortress.FortressLibrary$…` (30 `DivisionByZero`, 55 `IntegerOverflow`, 11 `IOFailure`, 2 `FileNotFoundException`, 1 `FailCalled`).
- Five of the carried types are objects in the one library, where the prelude has traits: `value object Boolean`, `RR32`, `NN32`, `Char` (`FortressBuiltin.fss`) and `object FlatString` (`FlatString.fss`). A hand-written class can extend a trait's generated `DefaultTraitMethods`, whose methods take `self` as a parameter and cast it; an object's class is final and its methods read `this`. The hack makes the five traits in the scratch library, each with `comprises { XCarrier }` and an empty object `XCarrier`, so that the checker keeps the exclusions that an object has (without the clause the apis fail the overloading check: 15 errors, such as 'Invalid overloading of || in trait FlatString: (FlatString, Char)->String and (String, Number)->String'). This breaks walk in the scratch tree, which binds these objects' natives.
- `FlatString`'s classes cannot be stubbed in Java under the component's name, since Java source allows no class `FlatString` nested in a class `FlatString`, and they are outside the package `fortress`, where a Java class of a named package cannot reach them. The hack names the component's class `fortress/FlatStringC`.

A real repair is a design first (the carriers: which class is a `ZZ32`, given `trait ZZ32 comprises { Int }` with `value object Int` in `FortressBuiltin`; what a `String` is at a helper; whether the five objects stay objects, with the code generator taught to let a hand-written class be an object's class), then about three rungs: the tables with the converters and the stores' carriers; the run-time classes with their stubs and the raise strings; the object carriers. PLAN sizes N5 as one rung inside the names batch.

### W3. 'Not in the trait table' (row 942), and the team's search hack

Past W2, `FortressBuiltin`:

    Exception in thread "main" java.lang.RuntimeException: Not in the trait table: RR64
    RR64 @ Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:291:7-9
        at ...TypeAnalyzer.typeCons(TypeAnalyzer.scala:884)
        at ...OverloadingOracle.lteq(OverloadingOracle.scala:71)
        at ...OverloadSet.fLessSpecThanG(OverloadSet.java:532)
        at ...CodeGen.generateTopLevelOverloads(CodeGen.java:7695)
        at ...CodeGen.forObjectDeclPrePass(CodeGen.java:4895)

Row 942's stack. It stops the whole component, not one declaration. `TraitTable.lookUpTypeCons` (`scala_src/typechecker/TraitTable.scala:76-100`) holds "A terrible search hack to try to get around the apiName bug. GLS 5/25/12": an unqualified name that the component does not declare is searched in the apis named `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `GeneratorLibrary`. So in the prelude's world the team's hack hides rows 940 and 942 for the prelude's types, and the switch removes that cover. The hack here: the same search over `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`. With it `FortressBuiltin` passes, and F-34's kind "Not in the trait table" does not occur in the measurement of section 3. A real repair is rows 940 and 942's root (the method index entries that lack their api), one rung; or the names batch extends the team's search and says so. No PLAN line names `TraitTable.scala`'s three prelude names.

### W4. `NN32`'s `zero` and `one` return `Number` (no row)

    Likely bug in static analysis, apparently malformed overload set not rejected for
    FortressBuiltin..NN32.one():Number
    # FortressBuiltin..(Integral[\NN32\] & {NN32}).one():NN32

`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:429-430` declare `getter zero(): Number` and `getter one(): Number` in `NN32`, which inherits `getter zero(): I` and `one(): I` at `I = NN32` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:682-683`). The getter's return type is wider than the inherited one's; the checker passes it (the distance is 0), and the code generator stops the component. Hack: `NN32` in both lines, which is also the library's repair. Two defects: the library's text, and the checker's acceptance of a getter that widens an inherited return type. See "For the ledger".

### W5. The declarations that the code generator refuses (rows 624, 81, 822, 812, 819, 315, 540, 875, 818)

Past W4, `FortressBuiltin` compiles whole. `FortressLibrary` stops at its first refused declaration ('Can't compile VarArgs yet', `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:307`). Section 3 counts them: 24 in 8 kinds, each kind in a row. Hack: the distance probe's tolerant code generator (`tools/distance/shadow-patch.py`'s edits of `CodeGen.java`) put into the scratch tree's `CodeGen`, so that a refused declaration is reported and left out and the jar is still written. That hack needed three repairs of its own, none of them a finding about the tree: a refused trait left its class writer in place of the component's, so the jar was never closed; a refused function left a half-written method, so each method is now kept apart until its class is written and one left open is written as a body that throws; and the wrapper generator writes its classes by another route, which had to flush the kept methods too.

Leaving a declaration out is enough only where nothing on a program's path needs it. Five refused declarations were on the path of a program that prints one line, and each needed a stub in the library's text (section 4).

### W6. One method written twice into a class (row 571's kind; 27 classes, 244 methods)

First load of the library:

    java.lang.ClassFormatError: Duplicate method name "MAX?0" with signature "(Lcom.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ32;)Lcom.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ32;" in class file fortress/FortressLibrary$ZZ32$DefaultTraitMethods

The code generator writes one name and descriptor twice into 24 classes of `FortressLibrary`'s jar (238 methods) and 3 of `RangeInternals`' (6 methods, `narrowToRange`). The compile reports nothing; each class fails when it loads. Row 571 holds one shape of it (an object that declares the meet of two inherited methods). The library's shape is wider: a trait that declares its own method at the instance of a generic supertrait's method, as `ZZ32`'s `<`, `MAX` and `CMP` beside `StandardPartialOrder[\ZZ32\]`'s and `StandardMinMax[\ZZ32\]`'s, gets a forwarder for each, under one name and descriptor. So the code generator does not see that the trait's own declaration overrides the inherited one.

The first hack, keep the first copy, ran `println` once and then, after an unrelated rebuild, sent it into a `StackOverflowError`: the copy kept for `ZZ32`'s `<` forwarded to `StandardPartialOrder`'s `<`, which calls `CMP`, which calls `<`. Which copy comes first is not stable from one compile to the next. The hack now prefers the copy that calls a static method of the class itself, the trait's own declaration: 98 of the 238 are swapped by that rule. A real repair: one rung at least, at the place where a trait's forwarders are gathered, with the override test at the instantiated signature; it first sorts the 244 by cause.

### W7. Missing casts that the JVM's verifier refuses (rows 307 and 695's kind; not counted)

    java.lang.VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack
      Location: fortress/FortressLibrary$QQ$DefaultTraitMethods.isFinite(Lfortress/FortressLibrary$QQ;)Lcom/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FBoolean; @1: invokestatic
      Reason: Type 'fortress/FortressLibrary$QQ' (current frame, stack[0]) is not assignable to 'fortress/FortressLibrary$Ratio'

`getter isFinite(): Boolean = (denominator(self) =/= 0)` in `trait QQ comprises { Ratio }` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:570`): the checker lets `self` stand where the comprised object type `Ratio` is expected, and the code generator emits no cast. It is thrown from `FortressLibrary`'s static initializer, at the first numeral coercion into `QQ`, so it stops every program. In `QQ` alone 23 lines pass `self` to `numerator` or `denominator`. Rows 307 and 695 hold the kind for a program's own traits; no row names the library's `QQ`. Hack: every compiled run of this probe had the verifier switched off (`-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:-BytecodeVerificationRemote`). So nothing below shows how many other methods the verifier refuses, and a count needs every emitted class loaded with the verifier on, which this probe did not build. A real repair: the cast where a value typed by a trait with a `comprises` clause meets a listed type (row 307's repair), one rung, and then the count.

### W8. `println` needs `WriteStream`, refused for its varargs methods (row 624)

    Caused by: java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Stream$WriteStream
        at Writer$stdOut.<clinit>(Library/Writer.fss:17)
        at fortress.FortressLibrary.println(Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4709)

`trait WriteStream` declares `print(args:Any...)` and `println(args:Any...)` (`Library/Stream.fss:70-71`), so the whole trait is refused ('OptionUnwrapException', row 624's trait form) and `stdOut` has no class. The library's own `println` does not call them. Hack: the two methods left out of `Stream.fss` and `Stream.fsi`. `FlatString`'s two calls of the varargs `assert` (`Library/FlatString.fss:63`, `:109`) were left out for the same reason. Row 624 is on every program's path: varargs must compile, or the library's text must change, before a line prints.

### W9. `Indexed` is refused for one `label` (row 81)

`trait Indexed`'s `indexOf` uses `label` and `exit` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2188-2194`, the `label` at `:2189`), so the trait is refused, and every string and every array is an `Indexed`. Hack: `indexOf`'s body made `fail(…)`; `Generator2.generate2`'s `label` loop replaced by its last line, the naive implementation (`:4983-4995`); the four postfix range operators over pairs and triples (row 819) made `fail(…)`, since the refused functions otherwise left methods that the verifier's stack check refused even with verification off. Behind `Generator2`'s `label` stands a second wall, 'Can't compile VarArgs yet', and behind `List`'s duplicate closure class likewise: a declaration counted at its first wall can hold more.

### W10. A closure class written twice into the jar (row 315's kind) stops `=` on two `ZZ32` values

    Caused by: java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/FortressLibrary$LexicographicOrder$RTTIi
        at ...FortressLibrary⚙$CMP⟦FZZ32⟧...the_function
        at ...StandardPartialOrder⟦FZZ32⟧$DefaultTraitMethods.=(Library/FortressLibrary.fss:232)
        at ...Indexed⟦FCharacter,FZZ32⟧$DefaultTraitMethods.isEmpty(Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2120)
        at fortress.FlatStringC$FlatString$DefaultTraitMethods.||(Library/FlatString.fss:126)

`trait LexicographicOrder` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2216-2228`) is refused, 'java.util.zip.ZipException: duplicate entry: FortressLibrary$\=fn@2227\!12-52??.class', and the dispatch method of `CMP` names every overload's trait, so comparing two integers needs its class. Hack: the jar writer keeps the first copy of a class. `List` has the same failure (`Library/List.fss:128`).

### W11. The dispatch method of a generic overloaded function names its component without the package `fortress` (no row)

    Caused by: java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: FortressLibrary
        at fortress.FortressLibrary⚙$seq⟦FZZ32⟧...the_function(Unknown Source)
        at Arr.run(Arr.fss:5)

`OverloadSet` builds the owner of a generic function's instance table and the name of its template class from `Naming.dotToSep(f.tagA.getText())`, the api's bare name, at four places (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java:904`, `:1361`, `:1724`, `:1728`), where every other place asks `NamingCzar.javaPackageClassForApi`, which puts a default library's classes in the package `fortress`. The prelude has no generic overloaded function that a program reaches this way; the one library's `seq` is the first. Hack, which is also the repair: the four places call `javaPackageClassForApi`. One small rung with its test, which needs the switch to be seen.

### W12. A carried type has two names at run time, its trait's and its carrier's (no row)

    Caused by: java.lang.ClassCastException: class RangeInternals$CompactFullParScalarRange cannot be cast to class fortress.FortressLibrary$Generator⟦fortress|FortressLibrary%ZZ32⟧
        at ...FortressLibrary⚙$seq⟦FZZ32⟧...the_function

A trait's generated `RTTIc` holds the trait's own interface class (`CodeGen.java:5999`, `cnb.classDesc`), so a static argument read from a value's run-time type is named `fortress/FortressLibrary$ZZ32`, while the descriptors of compiled code name the same type by its carrier, `FZZ32`. The dispatch of the generic `seq` infers `E` from the range's `Generator[\ZZ32\]` and instantiates `Generator⟦FortressLibrary$ZZ32⟧`, which is not the `Generator⟦FZZ32⟧` that the range implements. The prelude has the same two names and never infers a static argument from a carried type's RTTI (its `GeneratorZZ32` is not generic). Hack: the generated `RTTIc` of a carried type holds the carrier class. Part of the carrier design of W2; with W13 and W14 it shows that the design reaches the code generator's naming, not only N5's tables.

### W13. The number objects below the number traits: `asFloat` has no body on a compiled `ZZ32` (no row)

    Caused by: java.lang.AbstractMethodError: Receiver class com.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ32 does not define or inherit an implementation of the resolved method 'abstract ...FRR64 asFloat?0()' of interface fortress.FortressLibrary$ZZ32.

`trait ZZ32` declares `asFloat(self): RR64` abstract and `value object Int extends ZZ32` gives its body (`FortressBuiltin.fss`); likewise `Long`, `UnsignedLong`, `BigNum` and, for the whole of `RR64`'s arithmetic, `Float` (146 lines, `FortressBuiltin.fss:61-206`). A carrier that is the trait's class has none of the object's bodies. Two hacks, one for each shape: `Float` made a trait with a carrier object, as W2's five, and `FRR64` put below it; for `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, `asFloat`'s body copied into the trait. Putting `FZZ32` below a trait `Int` in the same way was tried and gave back W6's wrong forwarder. A real repair is the carrier design's answer for a trait with one comprised object.

### W14. A trait or object that extends a carried type gets the carrier class as its superinterface (no row)

    Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ClassCircularityError: com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ

`NamingCzar.extendsClauseToInterfaces` (`NamingCzar.java:799-824`) names each parent by `jvmTypeDesc`, which answers a carried type's carrier class, so `Float extends RR64` became an interface that extends the class `FRR64`. In the prelude nothing extends a carried trait in Fortress source. Hack: a carried type in an `extends` clause is named by its own interface. This wall was met only because W13's hack made `Float` a trait below `RR64`; an object below a carried trait takes the same path. Part of the carrier design.

### W15. An array of rank 2: an abstract method over an index type that is a tuple has no implementation (row 832's kind)

    Caused by: java.lang.AbstractMethodError: Receiver class fortress.FortressLibrary$__DefaultMatrix⟦FRR64,3,4⟧ does not define or inherit an implementation of the resolved method 'abstract Tuple⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧ offset(Tuple⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧)' of interface fortress.FortressLibrary$ReadableArray⟦FRR64,Tuple⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧⟧
        at ...Array⟦FRR64,Tuple⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧⟧$DefaultTraitMethods._[_]:=(Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2369)

`Array[\E,I\]` declares `offset(i:I): I` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2314`); `Array2` gives `offset(t1:(ZZ32,ZZ32)):(ZZ32,ZZ32)` (`:2847`). At `I = (ZZ32,ZZ32)` the abstract method takes one boxed tuple, and the body written at the tuple type was compiled with another descriptor, with no bridge between them. So `m[i,j] := x` and `m[i,j]` die on every rank-2 and rank-3 array, a `Matrix` among them. Row 832 holds the nearest shape (a generic dotted method whose single parameter has a tuple type from a tuple static argument). **No hack gets past it: it needs the code generator to emit the bridge, a rung's real work. The probe stops on this line here.**

### W16. The library's vector algebra: a generic method inherited from an api's trait has no body on the object (rows 495 and 732's kind)

    Caused by: java.lang.AbstractMethodError: Receiver class RangeInternals$CompactFullParScalarRange does not define or inherit an implementation of the resolved method 'abstract java.lang.Object map⟦…⟧(long, java.lang.String)' of interface fortress.FortressLibrary$Indexed⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧.
        at ...ReadableArray⟦FRR64,FZZ32⟧$DefaultTraitMethods.indexValuePairs(Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2288)
        at ...FortressLibrary$fn@2716...apply(Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2716)
        at ...__bigOperator...

`a DOT b` on two `Vector[\RR64,1000\]` values reaches `Indexed`'s generic method `map[\R\]` on a range object of `RangeInternals`, which has no implementation of it: the object inherits the generic method's body from a trait of another component's api. PLAN's phase 4 names this arm ("an object's inherited generic method … dies at the generic arm", from the generic-`distribute` probe) and phase 5 names rows 495 and 496. **No hack was tried: it is the code generator's generic dotted methods, a rung's real work.** Every `map`, `ivmap` and `DOT` of microGPT's vocabulary is on it.

<!-- Probe Y of the plan review of 2026-11-10 (its section 7.4), run 2026-11-13 by a Fable worker: whether one build of the tree can compile and run a program against the compiler's prelude and against the interpreter's library, with the prelude's run-time value classes kept and a second, re-parented set beside them; done in a scratch worktree, `/home/user/fortress-probe-y`, seeded from the base build `/home/user/fortress-base32` (`832f7d0d91`) with the rehearsal's patch applied; it works, and this note gives what ran, how the library is selected, every hack, the walls, the cost of the second set and an estimate in rungs; nothing here lands, and the scratch tree's whole diff is `probe-y.patch` beside this report. -->

# Probe Y: one build, two libraries

**The answer: yes.** One `ant compileAll` of the scratch tree gives a build that compiles and runs the one-line program against the compiler's prelude, as today, and against the interpreter's library, chosen by one environment variable at the compile and at the run. The rehearsal's `Array1` program and its dot loop also run against the interpreter's library in that build, by hand and through the test harness. A sample of the compiled tests passes against the prelude in the same build. No wall stopped the probe.

The base is `832f7d0d91`, the rehearsal's. "The rehearsal" is `switch-rehearsal.md`, beside this note; its walls are W1 to W16 and its hacks 1 to 12. "The review" is `explorations/reviews/plan-review-2026-11-10.md`. "The one library" is the interpreter's library.

Machine: nproc 4, Intel Xeon Processor @ 2.10GHz, OpenJDK 25, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` for the runs by hand and 4 in the harness. Another workflow ran beside the probe; the load was 0.2 at the first build and up to 9.8 later. No timing here is a pair.

## 1. What ran

All in `/home/user/fortress-probe-y`, after one `ant compileAll` (43 s, `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`) and the two library orders (section 5).

The three programs are the rehearsal's by its description (its section 4); its files were not kept, so they were written again. `Hello` is `run(): () = println("Hello, one library")`.

**The prelude** (no variable set, the tree's own `default_repository/caches`):

    $ ../../bin/fortress compile Hello.fss ; ../../bin/fortress run Hello
    Hello, one library                         (both exit 0)
    $ ../../bin/fortress compile Arr.fss
    Arr.fss:5:6-10: Array1 is undefined.       (exit 255; Dot.fss alike, 2 errors)

`Arr` and `Dot` cannot compile against the prelude in any build: it has no array type (row 305).

**The one library** (`FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, `FORTRESS_CACHES=<tree>/default_repository/caches-one`, and for each run the rehearsal's flags that switch the verifier off, its W7):

    $ ../../bin/fortress compile Hello.fss ; ../../bin/fortress run Hello
    Hello, one library
    $ ../../bin/fortress compile Arr.fss ; ../../bin/fortress run Arr
    a[5] = 25
    $ ../../bin/fortress compile Dot.fss ; ../../bin/fortress run Dot
    dot = 499500.0                             (every command exit 0)

With `-verbose:class`, the prelude's run of `Hello` loads no class whose name holds `FortressLibrary`, `FortressBuiltin` or `FlatStringC`, and the one library's run loads none whose name holds `CompilerBuiltin` or `CompilerLibrary` (each count 0).

**Through the harness, against the one library.** Three `.test` files (`link`, `run`, `run_out_contains=` the line above) for the three programs, in one `fortress junit` run with the same three settings:

    . run .../ArrOne (1375ms) a[5] = 25
    . run .../DotOne (1826ms) dot = 499500.0
    OK (6 tests)                               (16 s)

**Through the harness, against the prelude, in the same build** (`ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`, on `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests`):

- Twelve files chosen for what the second set touches (helpers that raise, the `NN32`, integer, `Char` and `asFloat` helper families, a caught `FileNotFoundException`, two `atomic` tests, one refusal of the code generator): `OK (22 tests)`.
- Every seventh file of the folder's sorted list, 125 files: `Tests run: 205, Failures: 4`. The four are `XXXFortToStringRungS`, `XXXGenericFunctionalMethodSelfSecond`, `XXXGenericTraitGenericFunctionalMethod` and `XXXPowNN64CompiledRungE`, each 'Could not load …: Resource not found'. The same four files run alone on the base build's code (`old-fortress.sh … junit`) fail in the same way, `Tests run: 4, Failures: 4`: a file with only a `run` step needs its sibling's jar, which a sample leaves out. So the sample shows no test that the second set disturbed.

**What did not run, and what was not tried.** The whole compiled tracks (1,907 tests) were not run against the prelude; the sample is 137 files of 876 in one folder. Walk was not run: the rehearsal's library text breaks it in a scratch tree (its hack 4), and this probe kept that text. A matrix, the library's `DOT` and microGPT stop where the rehearsal stopped (its W15, W16 and section 4); nothing here changes that. The cheaper form that the carriers' review proposes (section 7) was not tried.

## 2. How the library is selected

One variable, `FORTRESS_LIBRARY`. Unset, everything is as today. With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`:

- **At the compile.** `WellKnownNames.compiledPathUsesOneLibrary` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/WellKnownNames.java`) reads the variable once for the JVM (or `-Dfortress.library=one`). `Shell.useCompilerLibraries()` (`Shell.java`), which every compiled-path command calls, points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` at the one library's names where it is set, and at the prelude's where not.
- **At the run.** `bin/fortress_classpath` puts `ProjectFortress/build-one`, the second set's classes, before `ProjectFortress/build`. `bin/run_classpath` builds on that script, so the run's JVM finds the second set's `FZZ32` first. The compile's JVM gets the same class path.
- **The caches.** A caches folder holds one library's jars and the programs compiled against it, so the one library has its own: `default_repository/caches-one`, named by hand in `FORTRESS_CACHES`.

One JVM serves one library: `NamingCzar`'s tables are filled once, when the class loads, as on the base (`NamingCzar.fortLib`). The harness fits this: its `run` step is a process of its own that inherits the environment, so a test track against the one library is the same harness started with the three settings.

### What had to follow the selection

### What had to follow the selection

| what | file | how it follows |
|---|---|---|
| the names of the default library | `Shell.java`, `WellKnownNames.java` | by the variable |
| the thirteen value classes, with `FValue`, `MutableFValue`, `Utility` and `FException` | `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/`; second set in `ProjectFortress/build-one` | two sets of classes under the same names, the class path chooses |
| the stores' carriers `FJavaArrayStore`, `FJavaRR64ArrayStore`; the stubs `fortress/FortressLibrary.java`, `FortressBuiltin.java`, `FlatStringC.java` | `ProjectFortress/src-one/` | in the second set only |
| the helpers' 99 raise strings, and the six of `FortressBufferedReader` and `FortressBufferedWriter` | `runtimeValues/LibraryNames.java`, one copy in each set; `Utility.java` calls it | the strings stay the prelude's; the second set's copy maps them |
| the compile's table of carried types (the rehearsal's 15 rows) | `compiler/NamingCzar.java` | entered only where the one library is selected, since each row also enters the type's bare name (`NamingCzar.b`), and a test's own `Float` or `Char` would be taken for a carried type |
| a carried parent named by its interface (W14); `FlatString`'s class named `fortress/FlatStringC` | `compiler/NamingCzar.java` | by the variable |
| a carried type's `RTTIc` holds its carrier (W12) | `compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java` | by the variable |
| the tolerant code generator (hack 7): refused declarations left out, a method written twice, a class written twice | `CodeGen.java` (four `catch` blocks), `CodeGenClassWriter.java`, `runtimeSystem/ByteCodeWriter.java` | by the variable: the prelude keeps its refusals |
| the search of the trait table (W3) | `scala_src/typechecker/TraitTable.scala` | does not follow: it searches four prelude apis, then the one library's two, and finds only those that the compile loaded |
| the run's copy of the table; the wrapper generator's converters | `runtimeSystem/Naming.java`, `compiler/nativeInterface/FortressMethodAdapter.java` | do not follow: each is keyed by a name that holds its library, so both libraries' rows stand together |
| the dispatch method's package (W11) | `compiler/OverloadSet.java` | does not follow: the rehearsal's repair, the same for both |

The classes of the build that link against a prelude class by name, found by reading the constant pools of `ProjectFortress/build`: the thirteen, `FValue` and `MutableFValue` (their `asString()` returns `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.String`), `Utility` (the constructor it looks up takes that type), `FException` (it calls `FValue.asString()`), and the prelude's own `FZZ32Vector` and `FStringVector`. Every other mention of the prelude in the run time and the helpers is a string.

**The second set is the first set under a map of names.** The rehearsal's re-parented classes differ from the base's only in the names of the generated classes that they extend, so the scratch build makes the second set's sources from the first's: `build.xml` copies seventeen files through eight replacements (`CompilerBuiltin.RR64` to `FortressBuiltin.Float`, `CompilerBuiltin.JavaString` to `FlatStringC.FlatString`, and so on, with `CompilerBuiltin.` to `FortressLibrary.` last) and compiles them with `src-one` into `build-one`. One of the eight is a whole clause: the prelude's `FRR32` implements `RR32` and `RR64`, the rehearsal's only `RR32`.

## 3. The hacks

Each is marked `PROBE Y` in the patch. The rehearsal's twelve are all still in the tree and are not repeated here; nine of them are now behind the variable.

1. **The selector is an environment variable read in two places** (`WellKnownNames`, `bin/fortress_classpath`). Proper form: one selector, say an option of the commands that the scripts pass on, or a mark in the program's jar that the run reads, so that a program compiled against one library cannot be run on the other's classes. Today a wrong pairing fails at load with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
2. **The one library's caches folder is named by hand.** Proper form: `ProjectProperties.CACHES` and the two scripts take the folder from the selection; `ant cleanCache` and the build's stamp know both folders. Today the build stamps and empties only `default_repository/caches`, so the one library's jars go stale without notice after an edit of the code generator.
3. **The second set's sources are made by string replacement in `build.xml`,** one rule a whole clause of one file. Proper form: it depends on the carriers' decision. If the two sets stay equal up to names, the map can stand as a small table; if the one library's carriers get content of their own, they are hand-written files in `src-one`.
4. **The raise strings are mapped by prefix** (`LibraryNames.exceptionClass`): `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$X` and `fortress.CompilerLibrary$X` to `fortress.FortressLibrary$X`. Proper form: a helper names an exception by its simple name, and each set's `LibraryNames` gives the component. That edits the 105 strings once, with no change of behaviour for the prelude.
5. **The guards around the rehearsal's hacks** (`if (!compiledPathUsesOneLibrary) throw __t`, and the like). They go when the hacks they guard are repaired.
6. **`Naming.java`'s table and the converters hold both libraries' rows.** Harmless by their keys. Proper form: they follow the selection as `NamingCzar`'s does, from one table.
7. **The build's stamp does not cover `build-one`** (`build.xml`, `implementationFingerprint`). Proper form: it does.
8. **The verifier is off for every run against the one library,** as in the rehearsal (W7). With it on, `Hello` dies as there: 'VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack … FortressLibrary$QQ$DefaultTraitMethods'.

## 4. The walls, in the order met

None stopped the probe. What was met:

1. **Each row of the compile's table also enters the type's bare name.** By reading `NamingCzar.b`, before any run; passed by entering the one library's rows only where it is selected. No row; it is a property of row 874's table.
2. **`Array1 is undefined` against the prelude** for `Arr` and `Dot`. Row 305.
3. **`b[i] := 1.0 i`, with `i` a `ZZ32`, is refused against the one library:** 'Ambiguous coercion in call to operator juxtaposition: of the declarations applicable to an argument of type (RadixPointNumeral[\2,1,10,10\], ZZ32) only by coercion, none is more specific than every other: ((RR64 & {Float}), RR64)->RR64; (QQ, QQ)->QQ.' The rehearsal met it on a model line (its "For the ledger", row 533's kind). Here it is a four-line program. It is on the scratch library, whose `Float` is a trait; `Dot` uses `asFloat(i)` instead.
4. **The prelude's bytecode is not the base's, byte for byte** (section 6). No row; row 430 holds the like for walk's messages.
5. **Four `XXX` tests with only a `run` step fail in a sample** on both trees (section 1). Not a defect.
6. **The verifier** (W7; rows 307 and 695's kind), unchanged.

## 5. What the second set costs

**Source.** Against `832f7d0d91` the patch touches 28 files (the rehearsal's touched 47): the 105 raise strings and the thirteen classes are back to the base's text.

- Hand-written and new for the second set: six files, 221 lines, in `ProjectFortress/src-one/`: the three stubs (174 lines), the two stores' carriers (32) and `LibraryNames` (15). The stubs and the stores' carriers are the rehearsal's; the switch-over needs them on either road.
- New for the selection: `LibraryNames` in the first set (9 lines), 2 lines in `Utility.java`, 43 lines of `build.xml`, 9 of `bin/fortress_classpath`, 8 of `WellKnownNames.java`, 7 more in `Shell.java`, and about a dozen guards.
- Generated, not kept in git: seventeen files, 638 lines. Kept by hand instead, the second set would be those 638 lines in git, to be edited beside the first set's on every change.

**The build.** `ant compileAll` after the edits, with scalac: 43 s; the skill's figure for a build after an edit is 25 to 60 s. With nothing changed: 7.7 s at a load of 9.8, against the skill's "about 4 s"; the second `javac` compiled nothing. `build-one` holds 101 class files, 432 KB.

**The library orders**, one after the other in this build:

    prelude, five compiles          25 s    (AnyType 4, CompilerBuiltin 12, CompilerLibrary 6, CompilerAlgebra 2, CompilerSystem 1)
    one library, fourteen compiles  204 s   (AnyType 18, FortressBuiltin 12, FortressLibrary 84, RangeInternals 41, the other ten 49)

The rehearsal gives "about 200 s" for the fourteen, and the skill "100 to 110 s" for the five; the five took 25 s here, on an idle machine. The one library's caches are 70 MB against the prelude's 16 MB.

**A gate.** By the figures on file and these: a second library order adds about 200 s to each gate (the review's section 7.2 says the same), once, since the tracks' JVMs fill private caches from it or beside it; how the ant tracks would share it was not built. A test track against the one library costs what its tests cost: three tests took 16 s in one JVM here, most of it the compiles. So the standing cost is of the order of four minutes a gate while the track is small, and grows with the tests moved.

**To keep.** While both libraries live: every edit of a first-set file reaches the second through the map without work, if the two stay equal up to names; an edit that should differ between them needs the file moved to `src-one`. Every hack of section 3 that becomes a mechanism (selector, caches, stamp, names table) is code that the prelude's deletion removes again.

## 6. A finding beside the question: the prelude's jars change with any change of the compiler

To see whether the second set disturbed the first, the five prelude jars of this tree were compared with the base build's, class by class, after the tree's path was rewritten in each class's constants.

    base build's jars against the base build's code, compiled again cold:        590 classes, 590 equal
    base build's jars against the base build's code over this tree's sources:    590 equal
    base build's jars against this tree's jars:                                  558 equal, 32 differ
    this tree's CompilerBuiltin, compiled twice:                                 312 classes, 16 differ
    the base build's code with -XX:hashCode=0, and with =1:                      312 classes, 18 differ each

The classes that differ hold the same methods in another order, and their dispatch methods test the same types in another order (`javap` of `CompilerBuiltin$EqualTo` and `CompilerBuiltin`). So the order in which the code generator writes methods and dispatch tests follows the JVM's identity hashes. The base's code gives the same bytes on each compile only because the default identity hash is the same sequence in each run; a changed hash mode moves the order, and this tree's code gives a different order on each compile. Which of the tree's edits unsettles it was not traced. The rehearsal saw the same for the one library ("Which copy comes first is not stable from one compile to the next", its W6).

For probe Y it means that a comparison of bytes cannot show that the prelude is undisturbed; the tests have to. For the work it means that a compiled test can pass or fail with the order (the rehearsal's W6 was such a case), and that no two builds of different code give comparable jars.

## 7. Doing it properly, in rungs

Given the carriers' decision, which stands first on either road:

1. **The selection as a mechanism**: one selector, the caches folder and the stamp that follow it, a mark that stops a wrong pairing, the second library order and a first test track against the one library in the gate, with `Hello` as its first test. One rung. It edits `Shell.java`, `ProjectProperties.java`, the scripts, `build.xml` and the gate's script, and no file of the code generator.
2. **The second set**: the stubs, the stores' carriers, the names table for the raise strings, and the set itself, by the map or by hand as the decision says; `NamingCzar`'s, `Naming`'s and the converters' tables from one table that follows the selection. One rung, or two if the carriers are written by hand with content of their own. This is the rehearsal's W2 work done beside the prelude's classes and not in their place; it is not work added to W2.

So two rungs, perhaps three, and the review's "2 or 3 more for the second set" (its section 7.2) holds or is slightly high: most of what the second set needs, the switch-over needs anyway. After these two, each of the rehearsal's other walls that only the switch shows (W3, W4, W11, W12 to W14) is one rung with a test on the one library, on `main`, under the gate.

**Against the carriers' review** (`explorations/reviews/carriers-ways-2026-11-13.md`, way C and its point on the review's 7.1). That review says, by reading, that "one build serves one library" holds only for hand-written carriers that extend generated classes, and that under its way C in form 2 (the code generator writes the carrier over a hand-written payload class that names no library) no second set is needed. This tree's evidence agrees in part and cannot tell the rest:

- It agrees on where the tie is. The two sets differ in nothing but the names of the generated classes that the thirteen extend, and the `String` in `FValue.asString()`. A payload class that extends nothing generated has no such name.
- It adds one thing that way C's form 2 must also free: `FValue` and `MutableFValue` themselves name the prelude's `String` in `asString()`'s result, and `Utility` and `FException` link against it. A payload class that extends `FValue` inherits that name. So "names no library" needs `asString()` taken out of `FValue` or typed at `Any`; by reading, not tried.
- It cannot tell whether the code generator can write a native object over a payload class; that is way C's own three rungs and was not tried here. The session's room went to the main result, the tests and section 6.
- If way C in form 2 is taken, rung 2 above shrinks to the names table and the tables' following, and rung 1 stays as it is: the selection, the caches and the gate's second order are needed in any form.

**What I could not learn.**

- Whether all 1,907 compiled tests pass against the prelude in this build. The sample found nothing; section 6 says why bytes cannot stand in for the tests.
- Which edit makes this tree's order of methods vary from compile to compile, and whether the variation ever changes a result under the prelude.
- How the ant tracks, with their private caches, would take a second library order.
- Whether walk, the count stage and the distance stage are untouched: they run the same build, and none was run. By reading, the guards leave them as they were, since they do not set the variable; the rehearsal's library text is what breaks walk here.
- Anything about a JVM that serves both libraries at once. This design does not try it.

## Decisions

- **Two sets under the same class names, chosen by the class path,** not a second set under new names chosen inside the JVM. The alternatives: new names (a second package), which every place that names a carrier would have to follow: the code generator's literals, `equalityRule`'s `instanceof`, the converters, the loader's tables; or one class that implements both libraries' interfaces, which Java's single superclass forbids for the springboard. Evidence: the run's class path is already assembled by a script with the caches first (`bin/run_classpath`), and the run is a JVM of its own. No decision of the curator covers it; the review's 7.2 says only "a second set … chosen by the world that the compile command and the run select".
- **The second set made by a map of names in the build,** not kept by hand. Evidence: the rehearsal's seventeen files equal the base's under eight replacements (checked with `diff`, one file needing the clause). It makes the cost visible; section 3 marks it as a hack.
- **Every hack of the rehearsal's put behind the selector,** also where it looked harmless, so that the prelude's compile runs the base's code paths. `OverloadSet`'s four names (W11) were left for both: the rehearsal calls them the repair.
- **A wider sample of tests in place of the byte comparison,** once section 6 showed that bytes vary on their own.

## Defects, drafted for the ledger

- **The order in which the code generator writes a class's methods and a dispatch method's tests follows the JVM's identity hashes, so the compiled prelude differs from compile to compile once anything moves the hash sequence.** Status NEGATIVE-VERIFIED; class implementation gap (code generator). Reproducer: compile `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss` cold on `832f7d0d91` twice, the second time with `-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:hashCode=0`: 18 of 312 classes differ, among them `fortress/CompilerBuiltin$EqualTo` (its `CMP` dispatch tests `Unordered` before `TotalComparison` in one and after in the other) and `fortress/CompilerBuiltin` itself. Without the flag, two compiles are equal. Seen on the compiled path only; row 430 is walk's sibling, F-232 the tree's hashes. Seen under the compile command with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` on the scratch library, where `Float` is a trait; the rehearsal's entry says the same of a model line and asks for a check on an unhacked library. This probe adds the small program, not that check.
- **`fortress compile` of a component whose jar is missing and whose analysis is cached writes no jar and exits 0.** Met with `old-fortress.sh`: the private caches were the base's copy, the five prelude jars were deleted, the five compiles exited 0, and `bytecode_cache/` stayed empty. From an empty caches folder the same five compiles write the five jars. The skill's `build-and-caches.md` describes "all five compiles exit 0 and a jar is missing. The cause is not known"; this may be that cause. Not traced further.

## Sentences of the specification made false

None: nothing lands.

## For FACTS

- **One build can serve the compiled path with either library: the prelude's thirteen value classes as they are, and a second set of the same names in a second class folder that the run's class path puts first; shown in a scratch tree on `832f7d0d91` with the rehearsal's hacks, where `Hello` runs on both, and an `Array1` program and a dot loop on the one library, by hand and through `fortress junit`.** It means the review's option A2 exists. No test holds it, since nothing landed; the commands and output are in section 1. The second set's classes equal the first's under a map of eight names (section 2).
- **The classes of the build that link against a prelude class by name are the thirteen value classes, `FValue`, `MutableFValue`, `Utility`, `FException`, `FZZ32Vector` and `FStringVector`; every other mention of the prelude in the run time and the helpers is a string (105 raise strings).** Shown by the constant pools of `ProjectFortress/build` on `832f7d0d91` (section 2).
- **The bytes of the compiled prelude depend on the JVM's identity hashes** (section 6): 590 of 590 classes equal between two compiles of the base's code, 18 of 312 different under another hash mode.
- **The one library's order of fourteen compiles took 204 s and the prelude's five 25 s, one after the other on an idle machine of 4 CPUs** (section 5). The skill's 100 to 110 s for the five was not seen here.

## Commands

## Questions for the curator

- **Which order of the remaining work: the review's A1 or A2.** This probe removes the doubt that A2 exists. What A2 costs beyond A1, by this probe: two rungs, perhaps three, about 200 s and a small test track in every gate, a prelude that lives to the end, and four small mechanisms (selector, caches, stamp, names table) that the prelude's deletion removes again. - **If A2: is the second set a map of names over the first, or files of its own?** It follows from the carriers' decision (`explorations/reviews/carriers-ways-2026-11-13.md`). Under a way whose hand-written classes extend generated ones, the map works today. Under way C in form 2 there may be no second set, if `FValue.asString()` is also freed of the library's name; by reading only.
- **Does the order of the code generator's output need to be made stable before the switch-over's work starts?** Section 6. With it unstable, two compiles of one tree are not comparable, and a wrong forwarder (W6) can come and go. The sources do not bear on it; it is a question of what the gate should be able to rely on.
