## 4. What form 2 met, in the order met

1. **`FZZ32$RTTIc` named by the run time.** A generic arrow's class names a static argument's RTTI as `<carrier>$RTTIc`, and its `ONLY` (`runtimeSystem/Naming.java`, `stemClassToRTTIclass`). Passed by a nested `RTTIc` in each payload class whose `ONLY` is the object's RTTI.
2. **A dispatch test reads `<payload class>.RTTI`** (`OverloadSet.emitInstanceOfNG`). A static field `RTTI` in the payload class, set from the object's, was tried first: a class-initialisation cycle left it `null` in one test ('NullPointerException ... because FRR64.RTTI is null'). The dispatch now reads the object's class.
3. **Two names for one type.** The generated RTTI named the object's class, `fortress|CompilerBuiltin%ZZ32`, where the descriptors name `FZZ32`: a closure's arrow made from RTTIs at run time was not the class compiled code made. The RTTI now names the payload class. This is row 995's kind under form 2. Its rule is the review's: "the stamped class is named by the carrier".
4. **Not met:** a stub, a class-loader order fault (the method handle loads the object's class without initialising it), a second set of classes.

What the rung needs beyond the probe: the canonical name kept in every place that names a payload object's type (the three above are the places that the tracks reached; a reading of the other sites that name an object's class is the rung's); the names table following the selector; the tests; and the run under two hash modes.

## 11. Varargs (row 624), the closure class written twice (row 315) and the intersection receiver (row 540), probed for the coordinator on 2026-11-17

**The stand-in.** A varargs part of a domain is one JVM parameter of the type `ImmutableArray[\T, ZZ32\]` of `FortressLibrary`; a varargs parameter becomes, before code generation, a plain parameter of that type; at a call, the plain arguments are pushed, each extra argument is compiled and dropped, and a `null` of the array's type stands in the varargs place. It makes no value: it shows only what the code generator meets once varargs passes.

What remains: the kind environment 4 (rung V), the closure class 2 (row 315), the intersection 1 (row 540), and those two.

**Row 315.** `LexSame.fss`, `(|xs| = |ys|) AND: (BIG AND [(a, b) <- xs.zip[\ZZ32\](ys)] a = b)` over two `List[\ZZ32\]`, the one library's form (`Library/List.fss:127-128`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` `LexicographicOrder`'s `=`), compiled under the selector, with or without the search: 'java.util.zip.ZipException: duplicate entry: LexSame$\=fn@5\!23-66.class', exit 1.     (** CONCRETE GETTERS
        Default implementations of getters based on abstract methods
        below. **)
    getter indices(): Generator[\I\] = self.bounds
    getter indexValuePairs(): Indexed[\(I,E),I\] =
        zeroIndices().map[\(I,E)\](fn (i:I):(I,E) => (toIndex(i),get(i)))
    getter generator(): Indexed[\E,I\] =
        zeroIndices().map[\E\](fn (i:I):E => get(i))

    (** CONCRETE METHODS
        Default implementations of most array stuff based on the above.
        The things we can't provide are anything involving replica. **)

    opr[i:I]:E = get(offset(i))

    (** Initialize element at index i with value v.  This should occur
        once, before any other access or assignment occurs to element
        i.  An error will be signaled if an uninitialized element is
        read or an initialized element is re-initialized. **)
    init(i:I, v:E): () = init0(offset(i),v)

    generate[\R\](r: Reduction[\R\], body: E->R): R =

    seq(self): SequentialGenerator[\E\] = seq(self.generator)

...

        if a0.bounds = s0.bounds then

        else

8:- **Where the base matters.** The base 157323e51 lacks rung A's slot API (`TXReadSlot`, `TXWriteSlot`, `FortressArrayStore`). This matters only for the store's init race (§7, row N7), which ran on f5aa647de alone. Walk's STM is byte-identical between the two (§2). On the base, walk's arrays reach `AtomicArray` through the old `PrimitiveArray` glue; on main they reach it through `ArrayOps`. They are the same cells (`compile-ladder/rung-array-store/REPORT.md:18`).
24:**Shape.** It descends from DSTM. Every mutable variable, mutable field and array element is a `ReferenceCell`. `AtomicArray` is one cell per element (`AtomicArray.java:26-37`). A cell holds a chain of `ValueNode`s, each with a value, a writer transaction, a set of readers and the older node (`ValueNode.java:23-34`). A transaction is a status in an `AtomicReference`: ACTIVE, COMMITTED, ABORTED or ORPHANED (`Transaction.java:36-46`).
26:- **Commit** is one compare-and-set from ACTIVE to COMMITTED (`Transaction.java:229-260`). A cell's `cleanup()` then reads a committed writer's node as the value, or as the value of the parent transaction for a nested commit. It pops an aborted writer's node (`ReferenceCell.java:87-121`). This is DSTM's "locator" scheme: the value is decided by the owner's status.
31:- **Strong atomicity.** Plain access outside `atomic` is isolated from transactions. A non-transactional read aborts any active writer of the cell (`ReferenceCell.java:166-171`). A non-transactional write aborts every reader and writer (`:134-140`). The team added this in "Fixes for atomic/non-atomic interactions" (1d6d275bb, chf, 2008-02-13).
35:- **Cost outside `atomic`.** Every cell access takes the cell's monitor and consults the transaction, and a write allocates a node, a `ReadSet` and a `CopyOnWriteArrayList` (`c4-parallelism.md` §6). The measured share was 0.8 % of allocation samples in a four-thread C4 run, not the bottleneck (`c4-parallelism.md`, "Measured, 2026-09-19").
58:- **Non-transactional access** is a plain volatile read or write of the cell (`MutableFValue.java:18-29`). Generated code chooses between the two at every access by calling `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`VarCodeGen.java:326-362`, `:483-546`; row 641). So **atomicity is weak**: plain accesses neither take nor check the lock (defect N2).
129:- The team never measured this path. In its text, every `inATransaction()` built a debug string, which cost about 34 % of a scalar loop (row 302, fixed by the revival).
231:- *Locking.* All of a cell's state is guarded by the cell's intrinsic lock (`ReferenceCell.java:87`, `:123`, `:163`), so its accesses are totally ordered: Goetz's "guarded by" rule. The cost is a monitor per element.
249:- *Volatile is stronger than the language needs.* Every plain access to a cell, and to an element of the `Object[]` store, is volatile (`MutableFValue.java:18`; `FortressArrayStore.java:47`, `:55`). The specification asks only indivisibility (`memory-model.tex:252-260`) and program order for accesses that "certainly access the same location" (`:285-286`). `VarHandle` opaque mode gives exactly that, bitwise atomic for `double` too and without fences; plain mode may tear a `double` (JLS 17.7). This matters for P-84's `double[]` store.
266:- **The per-access transaction check.** It stays on mutable locals (row 641, F-12). For elements, the `Object[]` store checks the thread and the current transaction on every `get` and `put` (`FortressArrayStore.java:35-37`). Whether the unboxed store pays the same is undecided (§8, D1).

### 1.4 Compiled: the STM (`runtimeSystem/Transaction.java`)

**Shape.** This is a different algorithm: one global sequence lock, buffered writes and value-based validation. In form it is NOrec (Dalessandro, Spear and Scott, PPoPP 2010), though the code cites no paper.

- **The lock.** `global_lock` is an `AtomicInteger`; an odd value means a commit is writing back (`Transaction.java:76`, `:120-158`). Each transaction keeps a `snapshot` of it.
- **Reads.** A read takes the committed value. While the snapshot differs from the lock, it revalidates every recorded read by value and reads again. It then returns an own or ancestral write if there is one, and records the read (`:212-231`).
- **Writes** go to a private `Hashtable` (`:287-297`).
- **Commit.**
  - A read-only transaction returns at once (`:301`).
  - Otherwise the commit takes the lock by compare-and-set from its snapshot, revalidating whenever that fails (`:306-310`).
  - A top-level commit writes back, and a nested commit merges its reads and writes into its parent (`:312-344`, with the team's "This is subtle" comment at `:328`).
  - It releases the lock to the next even value (`:346`).
- **Conflict policy.** The committer wins; there is no contention manager. The generated handler retries without bound and calls `delayTransaction` (`CodeGen.java:1774-1802`). That backs off only when `FORTRESS_EXP_BACKOFF` is set; its default is off, "no evidence that it helps" (`FortressExecutable.java:33`, `BaseTask.java:214-230`).
- **Non-transactional access** is a plain volatile read or write of the cell (`MutableFValue.java:18-29`). Generated code chooses between the two at every access by calling `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`VarCodeGen.java:326-362`, `:483-546`; row 641). So **atomicity is weak**: plain accesses neither take nor check the lock (defect N2).
- `TransactionRecord.java` is an unused placeholder: `TXAbort` throws "Placeholder for now" (`:34-36`).

### 1.5 Compiled: arrays inside transactions (`compiler/runtimeValues/FortressArrayStore.java`, batch 28)

- **The `Object[]` store.** Inside a transaction, `get` and `put` go to `TXReadSlot` and `TXWriteSlot`, keyed by the array and the index (`FortressArrayStore.java:45-57`, `Transaction.java:31-62`). Outside one, they are `VarHandle` volatile accesses. `init` is a compare-and-set from null outside a transaction, and a transactional read-then-write inside one (`:60-66`).
- **The `double[]` store** (`FortressRR64ArrayStore.java`) "takes no part in a transaction" (its header comment).
- **The prelude's `ZZ32Vector`** is a plain `int[]` with no transaction check (`FZZ32Vector.java:18`, `simpleIntVector.java:26-29`). That is defect N8.

### 1.6 The code generator's `atomic`

`forAtomicBlock` registers its exception-table entry before it emits the body (`CodeGen.java:1783`), so an outer block's handler precedes an inner one's (rows 934, 937; row 888 is the same for `try`). Its other gaps:

- It catches only `TransactionAbortException` (`:1780`), so a Fortress exception leaves the transaction pushed (row 324).
- It has no case for `AtomicExpr` or `TryAtomicExpr` (rows 875, 353).
- Mutable fields bypass the transaction (`VarCodeGen.java:209`, `:220`; row 319).

### 3.3 Cost of the compiled STM (`runcost.sh`, machine in §0)

```
CCostSeq t=1: round 3 : plain 15 ns/op, atomic 208 ns/op, c = 4000000
CCostPar1 t=1: round 3 : 225 ns/op            CCostPar1 t=4: round 3 : 351 ns/op
CCostPar1 t=4: Had to retry a transaction 475225 times
CCostPar4 t=4: round 3 : 526 ns/op, 330760 retries   (four variables, no better)
CCostFree t=1: round 3 : 176 ms               CCostFree t=4: round 3 : 66 ms
```

- An uncontended block costs about 210 ns, against 15 ns for the plain increment. Rounds 2 and 3 agree.
- A contended counter is **slower at four threads than at one** (351–602 against 225–335 ns per update, over three rounds). All commits pass one global lock, and every commit sends every running transaction back to revalidate.
- The retry tally is a lower bound: workers add to it without synchronization (`FortressTaskRunnerGroup.java:37`).
- Private work with no shared state speeds up 2.0–2.7× on four workers. **The pool works; the STM does not scale.**
- The JVM's pool reported `parallelism = 4, size = 5` (the statistics line): `ForkJoinPool` adds compensation threads while workers block in `join`.

## Questions for the curator (decisions not taken)

- **D1. Arrays of unboxed numbers and `atomic` (P-84, P-169).** P-169's own reason is that "a compiled atomic write into any array needs that keying". Today the slot API keys only `Object[]`, the `double[]` store "takes no part in a transaction", and N8 shows what an untracked store does under `atomic`. The options:
  - (a) Unboxed stores stay outside transactions. This is recorded as a departure in Appendix I. It contradicts P-169's reason.
  - (b) A primitive slot API, `TXReadDouble` and `TXWriteDouble`, validated by raw bits (NaN and -0.0 make `!=` wrong), plus a per-element check of about 1–2 ns (row 641's rate).
  - (c) The library checks once per bulk operation, `fill`, `map` or `mul`, and picks a transactional or a plain loop.

  There is no default on record. microGPT needs none of (b) or (c) for correctness.
- **D2. Strong atomicity on the compiled path** (N2; `atomic.tex:100-106`). The options:
  - (a) Keep weak atomicity for programs outside the discipline, recorded in Appendix I.
  - (b) Plain writes of mutable variables take the sequence lock: a compare-and-set pair per plain write.
  - (c) The specification's shared and local objects (`shared-local.tex`), so that only shared objects pay.

  Disciplined programs, microGPT among them, are unaffected by (a).
- **D3. Parallel reductions on the compiled path** (N5). The options:
  - (a) The code generator forks call arguments by `ParallelismAnalyzer`, as it does tuples.
  - (b) The one library's `generate` binds its halves as a tuple.
  - (c) Leave them sequential until PLAN's "compiled parallelism" (inventory B1 steps 20 and 21).

  This bears on PLAN's order.

What the loop does, read in its bytecode (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 5): the `seq` loop becomes the compiler prelude's `countedseqloop`, which runs the iterations in order by a recursive split over boxed indices, with a closure call per element; each value is boxed (F-11); and the accumulator is a volatile cell whose read and write each first call `BaseTask.inATransaction`, as for every mutable local (F-40, what a size costs at run time, whose sized loop pays the same check). Within the boxing and the cell, the report counts four allocations per iteration, an interface call to the native wrapper and the casts, the part that unboxed doubles and `double[]` would attack. FACTS.md:215
- F-129 **A size is carried at run time as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`, and a program whose sizes are known at compile time loads, dispatches and runs compiled, apart from the open cases below.** It builds P-41. Each size value, such as the 3 of `Vec[\3\]`, has one descriptor; in a run-time subtype test, it is a supertype only of an equal size. A size read as a value is a `ZZ32` that the class loader writes in: `FZZ32.make` of an `int`, or, beyond 31 bits, `FZZ32.makeSize` of its digits, a `java.lang.Error` at run time that no `catch` sees (row 962; `runtimeSystem/MethodInstantiater.java:225-237`, by reading). Closures and tasks capture a size as a free static parameter (F-135). A size made from a number known only at run time does not run compiled: `tests/NatReflectTest.fss` stops at load (row 307). Gated by `compiler_tests/NatRt*`. Also open on the compiled path: a `ZZ32Vector` passed to a generic constructor fails at load (row 408); a dispatched overload arm whose static parameter has a concrete generic bound stops the compile in its sized form and dies at load in its type form (row 413); an object that extends two instantiations of one trait, one at a static parameter, passes the checker and dies at load (row 414). Row 416 is walk's defect: walk refuses at load `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])`, which the compiled run dispatches, since walk's overloading check applies no exclusion of instantiations. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-size-runtime/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 9.

- F-40 **Measured on 2026-09-24 for two size designs that were not built, a size cost a few kilobytes at load and nothing in a hot loop, and only the overload dispatcher read a size off a value.** The two designs were design A, descriptor classes stamped for each size of each generic, and design B, a class for each number, passed to the generic's descriptor factory; both ran on the size probes' private build (`perf-probes/nat/size-cost.md` section 1). The built design, one descriptor object per size value from `RTTIsize.of` (F-129), is neither, and nobody has measured its load size or its loops. Under either design, a size's classes came to a few kilobytes, against the 8.6 MB of classes that every run loads. A loop bounded by the size constant was not measurably faster than one bounded by the storage's length read at run time. The loop cost about 31 ns per element, which the bytecode shows going to a transaction check on each read and write of a local, to boxing, and to a method call for each element read. Once C2 compiles a hot loop, a native helper's call is inlined whole and costs nothing, and the boxes of its mutable variables stay (F-301). A call dispatched on a size cost about 4 to 20 ns more than the same call that the checker resolved at compile time. The built design's rung measured only the dispatcher's lookup of a literal size's descriptor: 0.9 ns on the landed build, its six runs from -2.2 to 7.0 ns, and 2.6 ns on an earlier build, on a dispatched call of about 23 ns. *Fortress revival · a teaching page · 17 November 2026*

# Arrays in Fortress

You asked how arrays work, and mainly how they'll run on the compiled path. Part 1 teaches the language and the interpreter, from small programs run under walk. Part 2 follows two of those programs into JVM bytecode, compiled against the one library, and from that bytecode to the design: where the boxes are, what each way to unbox would change, and what stands before a compiled array program runs on `main`. Each program on the page ran today, and its output is shown as it printed.

## 1. The short answers

**The language and the interpreter**

- **Half language, half library.** The literal `[1 2 3]` and the shorthand `ZZ32[3]` are the language’s. The types behind them, `Array1`, `Vector` and `Matrix`, are the library’s.
- **The sizes ride in the type on both paths.** Walk checks them as a line runs. The compiled checker checks them before the compile.
- **Every element today is boxed**, a number wrapped in a heap object. The bare-double store that “nothing chooses” is the team’s immutable `RR64` array: no factory returns it.

**The compiled path**

- **The compiler makes the library’s arrays as it makes any library code.** Each generic trait and object becomes one template class. The class loader makes the class of each instance, such as `__DefaultVector⟦FRR64,1000⟧`, the first time a program uses it, with the sizes in its name. Where a body reads a size, the loader writes in the number.
- **`a[i] := v` is ⟪N⟫ calls deep.** The subscript operator, a bounds check against the size, the vector, the primitive array, the store’s trait, a generated wrapper, a Java helper, and the Java store, which asks whether a transaction is open.
- **Each element is an `FRR64` box in an `Object[]`.** Once a loop is hot, the JIT removes a temporary box. It can’t remove an element’s box, or the box assigned to a mutable variable each iteration.
- **Five ways on file give a number array an unboxed store, and three say where the arithmetic runs on bare doubles.** Only the class loader’s way, the team’s direction, changes no library line, and nothing of it exists: the team left an empty stub in the loader and an unused plan.
- **The first array program to run** is the smallest of the switch-over rehearsal, a trial in a throwaway tree. The switch-over moves the compiled path, the compile to JVM bytecode, onto the one library, the interpreter’s library. The program makes an array of 8 `ZZ32` with the library’s factory, writes `i i` into each element, and prints `a[5] = 25`. After the second run, the second launch, of the batch now landing, it compiles against the one library on `main`. It runs in the batch after, once that library compiles whole to bytecode. In this page’s scratch tree it ⟪ran / reached⟫ (section 6).
- **You need to do nothing now.** An array is library code: Fortress traits and objects over a store, the object that holds the elements. The open array decisions are about speed and the model’s own types, not about running.
- **The rehearsal’s loop was about 100 times slower than Java.** Boxing explains 6 to 7 of that. The rest has no measured share.
- **Boxed numbers now change no array decision.** A bare-double store alone buys nothing while each read still makes a box.

**References**

1. The program, its compile and its run: [CLIMB-BATCH-33.md](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-33.md), section 2, “R. A method found by its interface”, “The measures” and “For the batch after, in this order”, item 4. The rest: the sections below.

## Part 1. The language and the interpreter

## 2. An array, written and typed

Start from the specification’s example, with a few lines added. `typecase` takes the first arm whose type matches the value as it runs, like Swift’s `switch` with `case is T`.

```
A: ZZ32[3,3] = [1 2 3; 4 5 6; 7 8 9]
println("A[1,0] = " A[1,0])
println("|A| = " |A|)
v: RR64[3] = [1.0 2.0 3.0]
println("v DOT v = " (v DOT v))
typecase v of
  Vector[\RR64,3\] => println("v is a Vector[\\RR64,3\\]")
  else => println("v is no vector")
end
s: String[2] = ["ab" "cd"]
typecase s of
  AnyVector => println("s is a vector")
  Array1[\String,0,2\] => println("s is an Array1[\\String,0,2\\], no vector")
  else => println("s is something else")
end
```

*Under walk, it printed:*

```
A[1,0] = 4
|A| = 9
v DOT v = 14.0
v is a Vector[\RR64,3\]
s is an Array1[\String,0,2\], no vector
```

- Spaces separate the elements of a row. A semicolon or a new line separates rows, and two semicolons separate the planes of a 3-dimensional array.
- `ZZ32[3,3]` is the specification’s shorthand for `Array2[\ZZ32, 0, 3, 0, 3\]`: for each dimension, a lowest index, 0, and a size, 3. That’s the notation on the number type that you saw.
- `A[1,0]` is row 1, column 0, counted from 0.
- One literal syntax gave a matrix, a `Vector` and a plain `Array1`. The specification lets the context decide. The library’s factory decides, by testing the element type against the eight number types.
- The overview’s `RR^3`, a vector of 3, isn’t built. Walk reads it as a type of its own. Today `v: RR64^3 = [1.0 2.0 3.0]` bound, and the `println(v)` after it stopped: “Couldn’t figure out Matrix [\RR64\]^(3) <: Object”.

**References**

1. The literal, its type and the shorthand: [aggregate.tex](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex#L117-L137), lines 117 to 137; the example, [Expr.Array.a.fss](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/SpecData/examples/basic/Expr.Array.a.fss).
2. The context decides, and `T^n`: [overview.tex](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/Specification/preliminaries/overview.tex#L735-L773), lines 735 to 773 and 934 to 938; [Overview.Expression.aggregate.a.fss](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/SpecData/examples/preliminaries/Overview.Expression.aggregate.a.fss), [Overview.Moving.fss](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/SpecData/examples/preliminaries/Overview.Moving.fss).
3. The factory’s test: [FortressLibrary.fss](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/Library/FortressLibrary.fss#L2842-L2856), lines 2842 to 2856; FACTS F-229.
4. `T^n` under walk: gap ledger row 24. The stopped `println` is today’s run, a shape that the row doesn’t name.
5. The run: `Literal.fss`, by `bin/fortress` in a worktree seeded from the base build at `c3b16ef2d1`, whose library equals `main`’s at `9f2ff9b04e`.

## 3. The syntax is the language’s, the types are the library’s

You took the array types for library types, and the literals for built-in syntax. Both are right. The language, its parser and walk, give:

- the literal, `[1 2 3; 4 5 6]`, and the shorthand `T[n, m]`;
- the subscript forms `a[i]`, `a[i, j]` and `a[i] := v`;
- static parameters, `[\T, nat n\]`, where `nat` marks a size that the type carries.

The library gives:

- `Array[\E, I\]`, with no size in its type. `I` is the index type: `ZZ32`, or a pair for rank 2.
- `Array1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]`, `Array2` and `Array3`, with a lowest index and a size for each dimension.
- `Vector` and `Matrix`, for numbers only, with their arithmetic.
- the factories `array1[\T, n\]()`, `vector`, `matrix`, and `array[\T\](n)` for a size known only when the program runs.
- the subscript itself: `a[i]` calls the operator `opr[i:I]:E = get(offset(i))`, as Swift’s `a[i]` calls the type’s `subscript`.

They meet at two names that walk knows: `Array` plus the rank, and `__builtinFactory` plus the rank. For `[1 2 3]` at a declared type, walk calls `__builtinFactory1[\ZZ32, 0, 3\]()` and copies the elements in. A literal with no declared type isn’t built today.

`Array1` isn’t in a component that you import, as `List` is. It’s in `FortressLibrary`, which every program sees.

In your frames: Swift’s `[Double]` is shorthand for the standard library’s `Array<Double>`. `RR64[3]` is shorthand for the library’s `Array1[\RR64,0,3\]`, with the size in the type. Scala’s compiler makes `Array[Double]` a JVM `double[]`. Fortress has no such special case yet.

**References**

1. The types and factories: [FortressLibrary.fsi](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/Library/FortressLibrary.fsi#L1612-L1637), lines 1612 to 1637, 1704 to 1816, 1851, 1893 and 1960; the subscript: [FortressLibrary.fss](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/Library/FortressLibrary.fss#L2384), line 2384.
2. The two names: [WellKnownNames.java](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/WellKnownNames.java#L30-L35), lines 30 to 35; [LHSEvaluator.java](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/LHSEvaluator.java#L119-L151), lines 119 to 151; the library’s word “enshrined”, [FortressLibrary.fsi](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/Library/FortressLibrary.fsi#L1787-L1793), lines 1787 to 1793.
3. A literal with no declared type: gap ledger row 49. `FortressLibrary` as the prelude: POSITIONS P-37.

## 4. How the sizes ride in the type

The library’s rank-1 array keeps no length field. It reads the size from its type:

```
trait ReadableArray1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\] ...
    opr |self| : ZZ32 = s0
    offset(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = do
        r = i - b0
        if NOT (0 <= r < s0) then oops(1, b0, s0, i) end
        r
    end
```

A product names a shared size once, so the shapes must match. An n-by-m matrix times a vector of m gives a vector of n:

```
opr juxtaposition[\T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat n, nat m\]
    (me: Matrix[\T,n,m\], v: Vector[\T,m\]): Vector[\T,n\]
```

A program that uses the sizes, with a 2-by-2 matrix to show that order matters:

```

run(): () = do

## 5. Where the elements live today

A `Vector[\RR64,3\]` from `array1` is three objects deep. The vector, `__DefaultVector`, holds a `PrimitiveArray`. That holds a store, a `JavaArrayStore`. The store holds the elements in Java. A 2-by-3 matrix holds one store of `s0 s1` cells, 6, row by row: a size can be a product.

- **Under walk**, the store is walk’s own `AtomicArray` of walk’s boxed values.
- **Compiled against the one library**, it’s the Java class `FortressArrayStore`, an `Object[]` of boxes such as `FRR64`. Inside `atomic`, each read and write of an element goes through the transaction. Section 7 follows one read and one write down to it.
- **Compiled against the prelude**, the compiler’s own small library, which `main` still uses by default, there’s no array type at all: “Array1 is undefined”.

**The store over a bare double array** is in `PrimImmutableRR64Array`, the team’s immutable `RR64` array in the one library’s `NativeArray`. Walk holds its elements in a `double[]`, and so does its compiled class, `FortressRR64ArrayStore`. It has `get` and `init`, no `put`. “Nothing chooses it” means this:

```

typecase im of
  PrimImmutableRR64Array[\3\] => println("immutableArray1 chose the double[] store")
  PrimImmutableArray[\RR64,3\] => println("immutableArray1 chose the general store")
  else => println("immutableArray1 chose something else")
end
r = PrimImmutableRR64Array[\3\]()
r.init0(0, 1.5)
r.init0(1, 2.5)
r.init0(2, 0.25)
println("the double[] store, named by hand: r[0] + r[1] + r[2] = " (r[0] + r[1] + r[2]))
```

```
immutableArray1 chose the general store
the double[] store, named by hand: r[0] + r[1] + r[2] = 4.25
```

The store works, and the factory doesn’t pick it. How a factory picks each element type’s store is your first open question.

**The prelude’s native arrays are something else.** The prelude has `ZZ32Vector`, over a Java `int[]`, and `StringVector`, over a `String[]`. The team wrote both by hand in August 2011. They have no type parameters, no size in the type and no `RR64` version. A `for` loop can’t run over one, and neither can be a type argument. Each read returns a new boxed `ZZ32`: the storage is unboxed, the traffic boxed. They go with the prelude, which is deleted at the switch-over.

# Arrays in Fortress

You asked how arrays work, and mainly how they'll run on the compiled path. Part 1 teaches the language and the interpreter, from small programs run under walk. Part 2 follows two of those programs into JVM bytecode, compiled against the one library, and from that bytecode to the design: where the boxes are, what each way to unbox would change, and what stands before a compiled array program runs on `main`. Each program on the page ran today, and its output is shown as it printed.

## 1. The short answers

**The language and the interpreter**

- **Half language, half library.** The literal `[1 2 3]` and the shorthand `ZZ32[3]` are the language’s. The types behind them, `Array1`, `Vector` and `Matrix`, are the library’s.
- **The sizes ride in the type on both paths.** Walk checks them as a line runs. The compiled checker checks them before the compile.
- **Every element today is boxed**, a number wrapped in a heap object. The bare-double store that “nothing chooses” is the team’s immutable `RR64` array: no factory returns it.

**The compiled path**

- **The compiler makes the library’s arrays as it makes any library code.** Each generic trait and object becomes one template class. The class loader makes the class of each instance, such as `__DefaultVector⟦FRR64,1000⟧`, the first time a program uses it, with the sizes in its name. Where a body reads a size, the loader writes in the number.
- **`a[i] := v` is ⟪N⟫ calls deep.** The subscript operator, a bounds check against the size, the vector, the primitive array, the store’s trait, a generated wrapper, a Java helper, and the Java store, which asks whether a transaction is open.
- **Each element is an `FRR64` box in an `Object[]`.** Once a loop is hot, the JIT removes a temporary box. It can’t remove an element’s box, or the box assigned to a mutable variable each iteration.
- **Five ways on file give a number array an unboxed store, and three say where the arithmetic runs on bare doubles.** Only the class loader’s way, the team’s direction, changes no library line, and nothing of it exists: the team left an empty stub in the loader and an unused plan.
- **The first array program to run** is the smallest of the switch-over rehearsal, a trial in a throwaway tree. The switch-over moves the compiled path, the compile to JVM bytecode, onto the one library, the interpreter’s library. The program makes an array of 8 `ZZ32` with the library’s factory, writes `i i` into each element, and prints `a[5] = 25`. After the second run, the second launch, of the batch now landing, it compiles against the one library on `main`. It runs in the batch after, once that library compiles whole to bytecode. In this page’s scratch tree it ⟪ran / reached⟫ (section 6).
- **You need to do nothing now.** An array is library code: Fortress traits and objects over a store, the object that holds the elements. The open array decisions are about speed and the model’s own types, not about running.
- **The rehearsal’s loop was about 100 times slower than Java.** Boxing explains 6 to 7 of that. The rest has no measured share.
- **Boxed numbers now change no array decision.** A bare-double store alone buys nothing while each read still makes a box.

## 3. The syntax is the language’s, the types are the library’s

You took the array types for library types, and the literals for built-in syntax. Both are right. The language, its parser and walk, give:

- the literal, `[1 2 3; 4 5 6]`, and the shorthand `T[n, m]`;
- the subscript forms `a[i]`, `a[i, j]` and `a[i] := v`;
- static parameters, `[\T, nat n\]`, where `nat` marks a size that the type carries.

The library gives:

- `Array[\E, I\]`, with no size in its type. `I` is the index type: `ZZ32`, or a pair for rank 2.
- `Array1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]`, `Array2` and `Array3`, with a lowest index and a size for each dimension.
- `Vector` and `Matrix`, for numbers only, with their arithmetic.
- the factories `array1[\T, n\]()`, `vector`, `matrix`, and `array[\T\](n)` for a size known only when the program runs.
- the subscript itself: `a[i]` calls the operator `opr[i:I]:E = get(offset(i))`, as Swift’s `a[i]` calls the type’s `subscript`.

They meet at two names that walk knows: `Array` plus the rank, and `__builtinFactory` plus the rank. For `[1 2 3]` at a declared type, walk calls `__builtinFactory1[\ZZ32, 0, 3\]()` and copies the elements in. A literal with no declared type isn’t built today.

`Array1` isn’t in a component that you import, as `List` is. It’s in `FortressLibrary`, which every program sees.

In your frames: Swift’s `[Double]` is shorthand for the standard library’s `Array<Double>`. `RR64[3]` is shorthand for the library’s `Array1[\RR64,0,3\]`, with the size in the type. Scala’s compiler makes `Array[Double]` a JVM `double[]`. Fortress has no such special case yet.

⟪BUILD: the layers, each with its javap cut⟫

**What the transaction does at an element.** `FortressArrayStore` asks whether the thread is a Fortress task with a transaction open. Outside `atomic` the answer is no, and the store makes a volatile read or write of the `Object[]` slot. Inside `atomic`, a read goes to `TXReadSlot` and a write to `TXWriteSlot`, keyed by the array and the index. The transaction keeps its own writes in a table, and records each read with the value it saw. At commit it takes one global lock, checks that each value it read is still there, and writes its table back. If a check fails, the block runs again. The `double[]` store takes no part in a transaction. Section 12 says what that costs and what is open.

## 8. Where the boxes are made, and where the JIT removes them

A boxed number is held in a heap object. On the compiled path an `RR64` is an object of the Java class `FRR64`, with one `double` field: Java’s `Double` against `double`. The code generator boxes every number. So `Dot`’s compiled loop holds no `dadd` or `dmul`: the multiply is a call to a Java helper, which does one `dmul` between an unbox and a box.

One iteration of `Dot`’s second loop, by its bytecode:

⟪BUILD: the boxes of one iteration, checked against javap⟫

**Where the JIT removes a box.** Once a loop is hot, C2, the JVM’s optimizing compiler, inlines the wrapper, the helper, `make` and the box’s chain of constructors. Escape analysis then drops each box that nothing keeps, such as the product’s. It needs the whole chain inlined. C2 inlines to a depth of 16 by default, and in the prelude’s loops a box’s constructor sat at depth 12. The one library’s chain of springboards is two classes longer for `ZZ32` than the prelude’s, so its margin is smaller. That’s by reading, not measured.

**Where it can’t.**

- An element’s box: the `Object[]` keeps it, so it escapes. Each element is an `FRR64` of 24 bytes plus its reference.
- The box assigned to `s` each iteration: the cell that holds `s` keeps it, 24 bytes an iteration.
- Any box that crosses a call C2 doesn’t inline.

**What the boxes cost.** Java models of the compiled boxes, against `double[]`:

- a dot product over 4K elements: 6.3 times;
- a 16-by-16 matrix product: 6.5 times;
- the row lift, a function applied to each row: 2.6 times.

An `Object[]` behind an interface, with a cast on each read, added only 1.6 to 9 %. The boxes cost, the generic container doesn’t.

A `double[]` store alone buys nothing while each read still makes a box. In the Java model, a dot product over a `double[]` read through a boxing accessor ran at 8.9 times the bare loop, against 6.4 for boxed storage. So where the elements live and where the reads and arithmetic run unboxed are two decisions.

**“Boxed numbers now”** means this. Your decision makes each built-in number type one value object, an object without identity that no type can extend, so that compiled code can later hold a `ZZ32` as a bare `int`. In the batch’s second run, rung N makes the prelude’s seven number types value objects. The code generator then writes each one’s class over a small hand-written class that holds the bare value, a payload class: `FRR64` keeps its `double`, and the class of `RR64` extends it. The boxes are the same boxes. What changes is that a value whose static type is `RR64` can only be that one class, which unboxing by static type needs (section 10). Code still passes boxes until the unboxing work, in the phase in which microGPT runs fast.

For arrays that changes no decision. Your decision fixes the goal: each number type’s array stored unboxed, in a Java array of its primitive type, with the sizes in the types now. In your words: “All arrays must have the most efficient and performant implementation possible. Otherwise it will remain a research toy, not an HPC language.”

Two checks run whether or not the code is inside `atomic`.

## 7. `a[i]` and `a[i] := v`, layer by layer

⟪BUILD: the layers, each with its javap cut⟫

**What the transaction does at an element.** `FortressArrayStore` asks whether the thread is a Fortress task with a transaction open. Outside `atomic` the answer is no, and the store makes a volatile read or write of the `Object[]` slot. Inside `atomic`, a read goes to `TXReadSlot` and a write to `TXWriteSlot`, keyed by the array and the index. The transaction keeps its own writes in a table, and records each read with the value it saw. At commit it takes one global lock, checks that each value it read is still there, and writes its table back. If a check fails, the block runs again. The `double[]` store takes no part in a transaction. Section 12 says what that costs and what is open.

## 8. Where the boxes are made, and where the JIT removes them

A boxed number is held in a heap object. On the compiled path an `RR64` is an object of the Java class `FRR64`, with one `double` field: Java’s `Double` against `double`. The code generator boxes every number. So `Dot`’s compiled loop holds no `dadd` or `dmul`: the multiply is a call to a Java helper, which does one `dmul` between an unbox and a box.

One iteration of `Dot`’s second loop, by its bytecode:

⟪BUILD: the boxes of one iteration, checked against javap⟫

**Where the JIT removes a box.** Once a loop is hot, C2, the JVM’s optimizing compiler, inlines the wrapper, the helper, `make` and the box’s chain of constructors. Escape analysis then drops each box that nothing keeps, such as the product’s. It needs the whole chain inlined. C2 inlines to a depth of 16 by default, and in the prelude’s loops a box’s constructor sat at depth 12. The one library’s chain of springboards is two classes longer for `ZZ32` than the prelude’s, so its margin is smaller. That’s by reading, not measured.

**Where it can’t.**

- An element’s box: the `Object[]` keeps it, so it escapes. Each element is an `FRR64` of 24 bytes plus its reference.
- The box assigned to `s` each iteration: the cell that holds `s` keeps it, 24 bytes an iteration.
- Any box that crosses a call C2 doesn’t inline.

**What the boxes cost.** Java models of the compiled boxes, against `double[]`:

- a dot product over 4K elements: 6.3 times;
- a 16-by-16 matrix product: 6.5 times;
- the row lift, a function applied to each row: 2.6 times.

An `Object[]` behind an interface, with a cast on each read, added only 1.6 to 9 %. The boxes cost, the generic container doesn’t.

A `double[]` store alone buys nothing while each read still makes a box. In the Java model, a dot product over a `double[]` read through a boxing accessor ran at 8.9 times the bare loop, against 6.4 for boxed storage. So where the elements live and where the reads and arithmetic run unboxed are two decisions.

**“Boxed numbers now”** means this. Your decision makes each built-in number type one value object, an object without identity that no type can extend, so that compiled code can later hold a `ZZ32` as a bare `int`. In the batch’s second run, rung N makes the prelude’s seven number types value objects. The code generator then writes each one’s class over a small hand-written class that holds the bare value, a payload class: `FRR64` keeps its `double`, and the class of `RR64` extends it. The boxes are the same boxes. What changes is that a value whose static type is `RR64` can only be that one class, which unboxing by static type needs (section 10). Code still passes boxes until the unboxing work, in the phase in which microGPT runs fast.

For arrays that changes no decision. Your decision fixes the goal: each number type’s array stored unboxed, in a Java array of its primitive type, with the sizes in the types now. In your words: “All arrays must have the most efficient and performant implementation possible. Otherwise it will remain a research toy, not an HPC language.”

## 10. The ways to an unboxed store, and to unboxed arithmetic

Your decisions set the goal and leave the way open. Unboxed doubles, and arrays of them, are required. Every number type’s array is to be stored in a Java array of its primitive type, `double[]` first, with the sizes kept in the types: “If this should have been high performance language, it cannot be boxed.” Each number type is one value object, so that compiled code can hold a bare `int`, `long` or `double`. Decision A, how a number type’s array gets its unboxed store, and decision B, where the arithmetic runs unboxed, are open, with no default, for after the switch-over. Their preparation, such as this page, comes before.

Each way below is put in terms of `Dot`’s classes and bytecode in section 7.

**What every store way but one needs first.** The tree has a Java store over `double[]`, `FortressRR64ArrayStore`, with its helpers and its library trait, `JavaRR64ArrayStore`. It lacks three things: a `put`, since the team’s only `RR64` array is immutable; a Fortress value that carries the store on the compiled path, which only the rehearsal’s hack has; and a Fortress object written for `RR64` alone, as `PrimImmutableRR64Array` is for the immutable case. With them, layer ⟪k⟫ of section 7 calls `getRR64` and gets a `double` back. Its wrapper boxes it with `FRR64.make`: a temporary box, which the JIT can drop. The write unboxes `v` with `getValue()` and does a `dastore`.

**Decision A, the store:**

- **A1, the library’s own type test in the factories.** `array1`’s `typecase` already tests the element type to return a vector. Its `RR64` arm would return a vector object written for `RR64`, through the library’s `cast`. One more template, instanced as `__RR64Vector⟦1000⟧`, with a size and no type in its name. `Dot`’s call `invokeinterface Array1⟦FRR64,0,1000⟧` stays as it is; the class behind it changes. The cost is one type test per array made, not per element. A probe checked and ran this shape on both paths, in the prelude’s world. The team: Jan Maessen, 2008, of the immutable `RR64` array: “these should be used in preference to the boxed version”.
- **A2, a plain `RR64` factory beside the generic one, chosen by dispatch.** The code generator writes a dispatch method for the pair, as for any overload. The same store classes as A1. It compiled and dispatched in a probe. Walk refuses the pair at load today.
- **A3, a factory name for each element type**, `rr64Vector[\s0\]()`. No test at all: the call site makes `__RR64Vector⟦1000⟧` directly. The model must name it, and `vector[\RR64,s\]` stays boxed.
- **A4, the class loader makes an `RR64` instance’s class with a `double[]` field.** This is the team’s direction, and your lean: “I would try to pursue the team’s direction unless we have a clear reason not to go there.” No library line changes and nothing selects. When the loader makes `PrimitiveArray⟦FRR64,1000⟧`, it would write a class whose `mem` is a `double[]`, with `daload` and `dastore` in its `get` and `put`. Today the loader can only rename: a field of type `T` becomes `LFRR64;`, and `[D`, the `double[]` descriptor, is no class name, so the copy keeps every number boxed. So A4 is new work in the loader and in the code generator, which must say which templates can be made so and give them bodies the renaming can’t. Nothing of it exists and no probe has run. What the team left: the loader’s branch for it, `if (false) { // Here will go all the magic expando-stuff. }`, empty since 2009; and David Chase’s plan, `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java`, 250 lines that list what to unbox (a primitive such as `RR64` as a `D`; an object without fields; unboxed fields; a `comprises` of unboxable types) and that nothing calls. A4 also needs one name per number type at run time, which the record’s row 995 says is two today. Even with A4, `a[i]` through the `Array1⟦FRR64,0,1000⟧` interface still returns an `FRR64`, unless decision B changes the descriptor.
- **A5, a special type**, an `RR64Vector` that the code generator lowers to a hand-written Java class, as it lowers `ZZ32Vector` to `FZZ32Vector` over `int[]`. No type parameter, no size in its type, not in the specification, and the model names it. It goes against keeping the sizes in the types.

**Decision B, the arithmetic:**

- **B1, Java helpers over whole arrays.** `Vector`’s `dot` would be bound to a helper that loops over two `double[]` in Java. One call per whole operation, and inside it plain Java the JIT compiles well. It needs an unboxed store from decision A, and it helps only whole-array operations: microGPT’s views read their elements one `get` at a time, boxed. The Java model measured boxed traffic over a `double[]` at 8.9 times the bare loop.
- **B2, unboxing by static type in generated code.** Wherever the checker’s type is `RR64`, the code generator keeps a JVM `double`: `s` a `double`, `a[i] b[i]` a `dmul`, `f(x: RR64): RR64` a method of descriptor `(D)D`. It boxes only where the value meets `Any`, a trait above `RR64`, or a type parameter. In `Dot`, the loop’s own arithmetic becomes `dmul` and `dadd`. The library’s generic code still sees `T`, so the read through `Array1⟦FRR64,…⟧` still returns a box, unless A4 or a store object written for `RR64` gives it a `D` descriptor. It needs the closed number types that your value-object decision gives, the payload classes of rung N, and the code generator’s second set of descriptors, which the team named in a comment and never built. It’s the team’s precedent, `Unbox.java`’s first case, and the largest code-generator work in the plan.
- **B3, both:** B2 for element access and arithmetic, helpers only where a whole-array kernel beats the JIT, as a measured remainder.

Peers: C# makes a class per value type, Java’s generics over primitives are a candidate proposal (JEP 218), Scala’s `@specialized` copies at compile time, and Haskell’s unboxed vectors pick a store per element type. They inform only.

## 12. The transaction checks

Two checks run whether or not the code is inside `atomic`.

- **On a mutable variable.** `var s: RR64` lives in a cell, a small object with one volatile field, `MutableFValue`. Before each read and each write of the cell, the generated code calls `BaseTask.inATransaction()`. Inside `atomic` the access goes to the transaction, outside it’s a volatile read or write. The record measured about 1 to 2 ns a check, and 64 % of a loop over an array with mutable locals, seven checks an element.
- **On an element.** `FortressArrayStore.get` and `put` ask for the current transaction on every call (section 7). The `double[]` store takes no part in a transaction, so an `atomic` write into it isn’t tracked. Which way an unboxed store takes part is open: stay outside, recorded as a departure; a slot interface for `double` compared by its bits, about 1 to 2 ns an element; or one check per whole-array operation.

The parallelism review explains the two transaction systems and what they cost. Another worker is writing a review of the ways to cut these checks, so this page leaves them to it.

1:#!/bin/bash
2:# seed-worktree.sh <base-worktree> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]
3:#
4:# Makes a worktree that is ready to compile and run Fortress without building anything, by copying the
5:# build and the caches of a baseline worktree that has been built once, and translating the parts of the
6:# caches that are keyed by the source tree's absolute path (explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md).
7:#
8:#   <base-worktree>  a clean worktree of this repository at some commit B, on which `ant compileAll` and the
9:#                    library-order recompile (explorations/repo-internals.md, "Compile order matters") have
10:#                    run, and nothing since.
11:#   <new-worktree>   where the new worktree goes; made by `git worktree add`, reused if it already exists.
12:#   <branch>         the branch it checks out: an existing local branch, else origin's, else a new branch
13:#                    cut from <start-point>, which defaults to B; `-` makes a detached worktree at
14:#                    <start-point> instead. Old-against-new runs need no copy of the base: tools/old-fortress.sh
15:#                    runs the base build itself with a private caches folder.
16:#
17:# What it does, in order: adds the worktree; copies ProjectFortress/build, ProjectFortress/.dependencies
18:# and default_repository/caches from the base; renames every file of the AST caches (analyzed_cache,
19:# interpreter_cache, interpreter_parsed_cache) to the hash of its source's new path (NamingCzar.deCaseName,
20:# compiler/NamingCzar.java:244-245; GraphNode.java:33 hashes the canonical path) and rewrites the base path

import re, sys
names = ["ZZ32","ZZ64","ZZ","NN64","RR64","NN32","RR32","Boolean","Char"]
for path in sys.argv[1:]:
    lines = open(path, encoding="utf-8").read().split("\n")
    out = []; i = 0; done = []
    while i < len(lines):
        m = re.match(r"value object (\w+)\b(.*)$", lines[i])
        if m and m.group(1) in names:
            n = m.group(1)
            hdr = [lines[i]]
            # the header runs until the line that closes the extends set
            j = i
            while "}" not in lines[j]:
                j += 1; hdr.append(lines[j])
            out.append("(* SWITCH HACK (arrays page): %s is a trait so that a hand-written run-time class can carry it; this object keeps its exclusions. *)" % n)
            out.append("value object %sCarrier extends %s end" % (n, n))
            out.append("")
            hdr[0] = hdr[0].replace("value object", "value trait", 1)
            out.extend(hdr)
            out.append("        comprises { %sCarrier }" % n)
            done.append(n); i = j + 1; continue
        out.append(lines[i]); i += 1
    open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8").write("\n".join(out))
    print(path, done)
EOF
